en: Praśastapāda’s Commentary.
Having bowed to the Lord, the Cause, and to the sage Kaṇāda,
the *Padārthadharmasaṃgraha*, which leads to great exaltation, will hereafter be proclaimed.
And that [arises] solely from dharma manifested by the impulsion of Īśvara.
Now, what are the categories such as substance and so forth, and what is their similarity and dissimilarity?
Throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion—these are the five types of action alone.

Because of the inclusion of "locomotion," such specific varieties as whirling, sprinkling, flowing, upward flaming, horizontal blowing, bending, and raising are merely distinctions within locomotion and do not constitute separate classes.
Generality (sāmānya) is of two kinds: the higher and the lower; it is the cause of the cognition of inclusion (anuvṛtti).
Among these, the highest existence (*param-sattā*) is a universal (*sāmānya*) alone, because its scope is vast and it is the cause of only positive concomitance (*anuvṛtti*).
Substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and the like are lower [universals].
Because its scope is limited,
and because it is also the cause of differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*), that universal (*sāmānya*) also receives the designation "particular" (*viśeṣa*).
(PDhs 2.2) Particulars (*viśeṣas*) are those that reside in eternal substances (*nityadravya*) and are ultimate.
Indeed, because they are the causes of absolute exclusion, they are specifically the "particularities" (viśeṣas).

The relation between things that are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*) and which stand in the relationship of the supported and the supporter (*ādhāryādhārabhūta*), which is the cause of the cognition "it is here," is inherence (*samavāya*).
Thus has the enumeration of the substrata (*dharmin*) been made without their properties (*dharma*).
All six categories possess existence (*astitva*), nameability (*abhidheyatva*), and knowability (*jñeyatva*).
And the state of being dependent [applies] to everything except for eternal substances.
Substance and the other four [categories] possess inherence and plurality.
Quality and the other five [categories] also possess the qualities of being devoid of further qualities and being devoid of activity.
Substance and the other three [categories] also possess a connection with existence (*sattā*).
Possessing both generality and particularity, being denotable by words whose meanings are established by its own convention,
and being the agent of dharma and adharma.
Being an effect and being impermanent belong only to those things that possess causes.
And causality exists elsewhere, except for [qualities] such as spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and so forth.
And [the quality of] being dependent on a substance exists in all things except for eternal substances.
The three [categories] beginning with generality (sāmānya) possess existence in their own right, are characterized by cognition, and are not effects.
The state of being without cause, the state of lacking both generality and particularity, and eternality.
And [the property of] not being denotable by the word "object" (artha).
Earth and the other nine substances possess substantiality,
the quality of being a producer within themselves, the possession of qualities,
and the state of being opposed by their effects and causes.
The state of possessing ultimate particularity.
And [the properties of] being non-dependent and eternal belong to [all things] other than composite substances.
Earth, water, fire, air, self, and mind possess multiplicity and the possession of lower universals.
Earth, water, fire, air, and mind possess activity, corporeality, priority, posteriority, and velocity.
Space, time, direction, and the self possess omnipresence and supreme magnitude.
And there is a commonality of existence for all that is conjoined.

Earth and the other four elements also possess the properties of being elemental substances (*bhūta*), being the material basis of the sense organs (*indriya-prakṛti*), and possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣa-guṇa*) that are perceptible by a single external sense organ.
The four [elements] possess the qualities of being the originators of substances and possessing tangibility.
The three [qualities] possess perceptibility, form, and fluidity.
In two [of these], there is heaviness and possession of taste.

The elements and the self possess specific qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*). Earth and water, along with the self, possess fourteen qualities. Space and the self possess specific qualities that are momentary and reside in a single part [of their substratum].
Space and time possess five qualities and serve as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for all things that arise.
Earth and fire possess occasional fluidity (*naimittikadravatva*).
In this way, similarity (*sādharmya*) should be stated for all cases, and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) from the opposite; thus, there is no confusion among the substances (*dravyāsaṅkara*).
Now, here, the dissimilarities [of each element] are stated one by one.
(Pdhs_4.1) Earth is so called because of its connection with earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*).
It possesses color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, and momentum (*saṃskāra*).

And these specific qualities, such as color and so forth, are established in this section on the application of qualities. By the mention of "visible," the seven [qualities] beginning with number are included.
From the teaching regarding falling, gravity is established.
From the mention of its commonality with water, it is a substance (*dravya*);
from the mention of subsequent ritual action (*uttarakarman*), it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*).
Odor exists only in earth.
Form is of many kinds, such as white and so forth.
Taste is of six kinds, such as sweet and so forth. Odor is of two kinds: fragrant and non-fragrant.
Its touch, being neither hot nor cold, is produced by maturation (*pākaja*).
It is of two kinds:
eternal (*nitya*) and non-eternal (*anitya*).

That which is characterized by atoms is eternal; however, that which is characterized by effects is impermanent. Furthermore, it is distinguished by the arrangement of parts such as stability and so forth, possesses a multiplicity of subordinate universals (*apara-jāti*), and provides manifold assistance such as serving as beds, seats, and the like.
And its effect is threefold:
that which is designated as body, sense-faculties, and objects.
(PDHS 4.1) The body is of two kinds.
It is both born from a womb and not born from a womb.
Among these, that which is not born from a womb arises for the gods and ṛṣis from atoms accompanied by a specific merit (*dharma*), without depending on semen and blood.
The bodies of punishment for small creatures arise from atoms accompanied by a specific demerit (*adharma*).
It is born from the union of semen and blood, and is born from a womb.
That is of two kinds: viviparous and oviparous.
Among humans, domestic animals, and wild beasts, it is viviparous.
The egg-born [category] consists of birds and reptiles.

(Pdhs 4.1[28]) The sense organ that manifests odors—the nose—is composed of earthy atoms (*pārthivāvayava*) that have not been overwhelmed by water and other elements; it belongs to all living beings.
As for its object, it is composed through the sequence beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), and is of three kinds, characterized as soil, stone, and plants. (Pdhs 4.1[28])
In that regard, the terrestrial regions consist of walls, bricks, and other varieties of clay;
stones consist of pebbles, gems, diamonds, and so forth;
and the stationary beings consist of grasses, medicinal herbs, trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and forest giants.
Water is so called because of its connection with moisture (*āptva*).
It possesses color, taste, touch, fluidity, viscidity, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, weight, and faculty (*saṃskāra*).
Their establishment is as previously described.
The color, taste, and touch of water are exclusively white, sweet, and cold.
Viscidity exists only in water, as does its natural fluidity.
These [qualities] are, as before, of two kinds.
Because of their being both eternal and non-eternal. Their effects, moreover, are threefold,
designated as body, sense organs, and objects.
In that regard, the body in the world of Varuṇa is exclusively non-womb-born;
it is capable of experience due to being supported by the constituent parts of earth.
The sense organ is the gustatory faculty, which manifests tastes for all living beings and is composed of water-constituents that are not overwhelmed by those of a different class.
The object, however, consists of rivers, oceans, snowflakes, hailstones, and so forth.
Fire is so called because of its connection with the nature of fire (*tejastva*).
It possesses color, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, fluidity, and latent disposition (*saṃskāra*).
Their establishment is as previously described.
In that regard, its color is white and luminous;
its touch is exclusively hot.
That too is of two kinds, due to its existence as both atoms and their effects.
And the effect consists of the triad beginning with the body.
The body is not born from a womb; it exists in the world of the sun and is capable of experience due to its support by earthly particles.

The sense-faculty (*indriya*) of all living beings is the eye, which is composed of fire-constituents (*tejo’vayava*) that are not overcome by other parts and which manifests form. It is of four kinds, designated according to its objects: terrestrial, celestial, digestive, and mineral.

Among these, the terrestrial [fire] arises from wood as fuel, has the nature of upward flaming, and is capable of cooking, burning, and sweating; the celestial [fire], which lacks fuel, consists of solar light, lightning, and so forth; the digestive [fire] is for the purpose of transforming the consumed food into chyle and other constituents; and the mineral [fire] consists of gold and the like.
In this regard, the perception of taste and other qualities occurs through inherence in that which is conjoined (*samyuktasamavāya*).
Air is so called because of its connection with the nature of air (*vāyutva*).
It possesses touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and impression (*saṃskāra*).
Its touch is neither hot nor cold, and it is not produced by heat (*apākaja*).
[The existence of] quality is established because [the Sūtra] specifies qualities.
By the statement "in the case of formless [substances], there is no visual perception," the seven [qualities] beginning with number are established.
By the mention of the action of grass, [the quality of] momentum is established.
And this [substance] is of two kinds, due to its existence as both atoms and effects.
Among these, that characterized as an effect is fourfold: body, sense organ, object, and vital breath.
Among these, the body of the gods in the world is exclusively non-maternal (born without a womb), and it is capable of experience due to the support of earthy particles.

The tactile faculty (*tvagindriya*) is that which enables all living beings to perceive touch; it is composed of wind-particles not overwhelmed by earth and the other elements, and it pervades the entire body.

Its object, however, is the substrate of the touch being perceived; it is characterized by the signs of touch, sound, support, and motion; its nature is horizontal movement; and it possesses the capacity for propelling and sustaining clouds and other such things.
Although this [wind] is imperceptible, its manifold diversity is inferred through its condensation (*sammūrcchana*).
Conjunction (*sammūrcchana*), moreover, is the collision of two air-currents of equal velocity moving in opposite directions.
That too is inferred from the upward movement of the air-currents, which possess constituent parts, and that [upward movement] is inferred from the upward movement of grass and other such objects.

Prāṇa is the single cause for the impelling and so forth of the elements of rasa and mala within the body; though being one, it receives the designations of apāna and so on due to the differentiation of its functions.
Now, the process of the creation and dissolution of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is explained here.

Immediately thereafter, within that very great ocean, a vast mass of fire arises from fiery atoms (*taijasāṇu*) through the sequence beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). Because it is not overcome by anything else, it remains intensely blazing.
In that [mass], the qualities (*guṇa*) of space (*ākāśa*) are sound, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction.

It is not a quality of the self because it is perceived by the external sense organs, because it can be apprehended by other selves, because it does not inhere in the self, and because it is perceived as distinct from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
It does not belong to space, time, or the mind because it is apprehended by the auditory organ and because it lacks the status of a specific quality (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*) of those.
Furthermore, it is eternal because it lacks both homogeneous and heterogeneous causes.
Time is characterized by the notions of priority and posteriority, succession and simultaneity, as well as slowness and quickness.
It is the cause of the production, subsistence, and destruction of all effects, because these are designated in relation to it.
Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction.
Its unity is established because there is no distinction in its temporal characteristics. Its plurality follows from its conformity [to multiple objects].
Its dimension is that of the supremely great, according to the statement that time is a cause.
Because it causes the destruction of that [conjunction], it is disjunction (*vibhāga*). Space (*dik*) has as its inferential mark the cognitions of "east," "west," and so forth,
because no other cause for such cognitions is possible.
Its qualities—number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction—are established as being like those of time.
It is called the "self" (ātman) because of its connection with the property of selfhood (ātmatva).
Consciousness does not belong to the body, because, like a jar or similar objects, it is a product of the elements, and because it is absent when the body is dead.

Its qualities are intellect (*buddhi*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), effort (*prayatna*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), mental impression (*saṃskāra*), number (*saṃkhyā*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and disjunction (*vibhāga*).

Merit and demerit are included because it is stated that they are not causes for the qualities of other selves; mental impression is included because it is stated to be the cause for the arising of memory;
and conjunction is included because pleasure and the others are produced from contact.
It is disjunction because it is the cause of that destruction.
It is called "mind" (manas) because of its connection with mentality (manastva).

Even when the self, the sense organs, and their objects are present, we observe that knowledge, pleasure, and so forth arise where they previously did not exist; therefore, another instrument (karaṇa) is inferred.

Furthermore, since it is observed that memory arises even when the ear and other [external senses] are inactive, and since there exists an internal object of apprehension such as pleasure which is not grasped by the external senses, it is an internal instrument (antahkaraṇa).
Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
Because of the statement regarding the non-simultaneity of effort and cognition, its oneness in each body is established.
Distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) is also established for this very reason.
From the statement of its absence [of parts], it has atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*).
From the statement of moving away and moving toward, there are conjunction and disjunction (*saṃyoga-vibhāga*).
Because of being corporeal (*mūrtatva*), there are priority and posteriority (*paratva-aparatva*) and momentum (*saṃskāra*).
Because it lacks tangibility, it does not originate substances;
because it possesses motion, it is corporeal;
and because it would entail having a common physical body, it is non-cognizant.
Because it exists as an instrument, it is for the sake of another;
because it possesses qualities, it is a substance;
and because it moves swiftly by virtue of being grasped by effort and the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).
Thus ends the category of substance (*dravyapadārtha*) in Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya*.
Now follows the determination of the category of quality (*guṇapadārthanirūpaṇa*).

All qualities, such as color (*rūpa*) and the rest, possess the connection with the universal "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*), as well as the properties of being dependent upon substance (*dravyāśritatva*), being devoid of further qualities (*nirguṇatva*), and being devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*).
The qualities of the non-material [substances] are color, taste, odor, tangibility, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, and momentum.
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, and sound are the qualities of the formless.
Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction are qualities common to both [substances].
Conjunction, disjunction, duality, dual separateness, and so forth, are dependent upon multiple substrata.
The remaining [elements], however, each subsist in a single substance.

Color, taste, smell, touch, viscidity, natural fluidity, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, and sound are the specific qualities (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*).
Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity caused by [heat], and momentum are the common qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*).
Sound, touch, visible form, taste, and odor are external objects, each perceivable by a single sense faculty.
Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, fluidity, viscidity, and momentum are perceptible by two sense-faculties.
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort, however, are perceivable by the internal organ.
The properties of heaviness, merit, demerit, and cultivation are beyond the reach of the senses.
Non-produced color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, oneness, individuality, heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, and speed have qualities of their causes as their antecedents.
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, and sound are preceded by qualities that do not have [other] qualities as their cause.

Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, sound, the dimension of cotton, subsequent conjunction, occasional fluidity, priority, and posteriority—these are produced by cooking; they are also produced by conjunction.
Conjunction, disjunction, and momentum are born of action.
Sound and the subsequent divisions are both produced by division.
Remoteness, proximity, duality, dual separateness, and so forth, depend upon cognition.
Color, taste, odor, non-hot touch, sound, dimension, oneness, individual separateness, and viscidity originate [their effects] from a genus similar to themselves.
Pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort initiate effects of a different genus.
Conjunction, disjunction, number, gravity, fluidity, hot touch, cognition, merit, demerit, and mental impressions are the initiators of both homogeneous and heterogeneous effects.
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, mental impression, and sound originate from that which is inherent in their own substratum.
Color, taste, odor, touch, dimension, viscidity, and effort are initiators of other [substances].
Conjunction, disjunction, number, individuality, separateness, gravity, fluidity, velocity, merit, and demerit are productive causes in both cases.
Heaviness, fluidity, momentum, effort, merit, demerit, and specific types of conjunction are the causes of action.
Color, taste, odor, non-hot touch, number, dimension, individuality, viscidity, and sound possess the nature of being non-inherent causes.
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impressions are efficient causes.
Conjunction, disjunction, hot touch, heaviness, fluidity, and speed possess the nature of being causes in both ways.
Remoteness, proximity, duality, dual separateness, and so forth, are not causes.
Conjunction, disjunction, sound, and the specific qualities of the self reside in a limited portion [of their respective substrata].
The remaining [factors] possess pervasiveness with respect to their basis.
Non-produced color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, singularity, individual separateness, natural fluidity, heaviness, and viscidity persist as long as the substance exists.
And for the remaining [factors], there is the state of not persisting as long as the substance exists.
Due to the connection of each of all the qualities, such as form and so forth, with its own specific generality (aparasāmānya), they receive the designations "form" and so on.
Among these, visible form (*rūpa*) is that which is grasped by the eye;

it functions within earth, water, and fire; it is the object of perception for substances and so forth; it assists the eye; it is of many kinds, such as white and so on; it is eternal in the atoms of water and so forth, but in the atoms of earth it is subject to destruction through contact with fire; in all produced substances (*kāryadravya*), it is preceded by the qualities of its causes; and it perishes only through the destruction of its substratum. Taste (*rasa*) is that which is grasped by the sense of taste.

It functions in earth and water; it is the cause of life, nourishment, strength, and health; it acts in conjunction with the sense of taste; it is divided into the varieties of sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent.
Its eternity, non-eternity, and production are also like those of color (*rūpa*).
Odor is that which is apprehended by the nose; it functions within the earth element and acts as an auxiliary to the sense of smell. It is either fragrant or foul-smelling.
Its arising and other characteristics are explained as before.

Tactile sensation (*sparśa*), however, is perceivable by the sense faculty of touch (*tvagindriya*). Its function consists in [the elements of] earth, water, fire, and air; it is the cause of the sense of touch and conforms to color-form (*rūpa*). It is of three kinds, distinguished as cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold.
Its eternity, non-eternity, and production are also as previously described.
The process by which color and other qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) arise in the atoms of earth is as follows:

when a raw substance such as a jar is conjoined with fire, actions arise in the atoms that constitute it, either due to the impact of the fire or its impulsion. From these actions come disjunctions; from the disjunctions, the destruction of the [original] conjunctions; and from the destruction of the conjunctions, the causal substance perishes.

When that [composite substance] has perished, the destruction of the dark color and other qualities occurs in the independent atoms due to contact with fire and dependence upon heat. Then, from another contact with fire and dependence upon heat, qualities produced by cooking (*pākaja*) arise. Immediately thereafter, through the conjunction of the self and the atoms—dependent upon the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of those who experience [the results]—action arises in the atoms in which the qualities produced by cooking have been generated. From their mutual conjunction, the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) arises in the sequence beginning with the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).
And therein, the production of color and other qualities occurs through the sequence of the qualities of the causes.

Furthermore, the production or destruction of color and other qualities cannot occur in a produced substance (*kāryadravya*) alone, because fire cannot pervade it—both internally and externally—across all its constituent parts. Nor can pervasion occur through the penetration of atoms, because that would entail the destruction of the produced substance.
Number (*saṃkhyā*) is the cause for the conventional usage of "one" and so forth. It is further of two kinds: residing in a single substance and residing in multiple substances.

In that regard, the production and the status of permanence or impermanence for that which consists of a single substance—such as the color and other qualities of water-atoms and so forth—are [the same] as those of the atoms themselves.
However, that which consists of multiple substances ranges from duality up to the highest number (parārdha).
Indeed, its production arises from unities accompanied by the cognition of multiple objects; its destruction results from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi). How so?

When, for a cognizer, upon the contact of the eye with two substances—one of the same class and one of a different class—there arises the cognition of the generality of unity (*ekatvasāmānya*) inherent in that which is inherent in what is conjoined (*tatsaṃyuktasamavetasamaveta*), then, from the cognition of the generality of unity and from the cognitions of the relations [of inherence], there arises a single cognition directed toward multiple objects regarding the two qualities of unity. At that time, depending upon that [cognition], duality is produced in the two substrates by means of the two unities. Thereafter, once again, the cognition of the generality of duality arises in respect to that [duality]. At that same moment, due to that cognition of the generality of duality, the state of the "dependent cognition" (*apekṣābuddhi*) is about to perish; and simultaneously, due to the generality of duality, its relation, and the cognition thereof, the cognition of the quality of duality begins to arise. This constitutes one point in time.

Now, following that: from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), there is the state of being about to perish (*vinaśyattā*) of the quality of duality (*dvitva*). The cognition of the quality of duality is the cause for the destruction of the cognition of the generality (*sāmānya*) of duality. At the same time, from the connection between the quality of duality, its cognition, and [the relation], the cognition of the substance (*dravyabuddhi*)—namely, "two substances"—is arising. This constitutes one single moment.

Immediately after that, there is the arising of the cognition of substance (*dravyajñāna*) regarding "two substances," the destruction of duality (*dvitva*), the state of the cognition of the quality of duality being in the process of perishing, and the arising of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) from the cognition of substance; these constitute one moment. Immediately after that, from the cognition of substance, there is the destruction of the cognition of the quality of duality, and also the destruction of the cognition of the substance itself from the mental impression. By this, the production of triad (*tritva*) and so forth is also explained:

their production is from the unitary cognitions (*ekatva*) accompanied by the cognition of multiple objects, and their destruction is from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).
"And sometimes [duality arises] from the destruction of the substratum. How so?

When an action (*karman*) arises in a part that is the locus of unity, at that very moment the cognition of the generality (*sāmānya*) of unity arises; by that action, disjunction (*vibhāga*) is produced from another part, and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises.

Then, at the very same time that the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is destroyed by that disjunction, duality (*dvitva*) arises; and from the destruction of the conjunction, the destruction of the substance (*dravya*) occurs, while the cognition of the generality arises.

Therefore, at the very moment when the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) perishes due to the general cognition (*sāmānyajñāna*), at that same moment the duality (*dvitva*) perishes because of the destruction of its substratum (*āśraya*). This formulation is sound under the view of "the killer and the killed" (*badhyaghātakapakṣa*). However, if there were opposition characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthānalakṣaṇa*), it would follow that the cognition of the substance could not arise.
How so?

Because if the duality were destroyed by the destruction of the relative cognition at the same time as the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*), it would follow that the cognition of the substance—"two substances"—which depends upon that [duality], could not arise.

If it is thought that, as in the case of inference (*laiṅgika*), [the cognition occurs] from mere knowledge—just as in the case of "the cognition of what has come to be from what has not yet come to be," where there is inference from mere knowledge even in the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*)—so too, even when a quality (*guṇa*) has perished, there would be a cognition of the substance (*dravya*) from the mere cognition of the quality;
[we reply: no, because it is a cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*).
For a cognition of a qualified object cannot occur through similarity (*sārūpya*) without a connection to a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

And thus the author of the Sūtras says: "From the whiteness inherent [in the substance] arises the cognition of whiteness; from that, the cognition of the white [substance]; these two stand in a relationship of cause and effect.

(PDhS 8.6) However, inferential knowledge does not arise without a distinction [between the mark and the object]. Therefore, this comparison is unequal. It is not because of rapid production, as in the case of the statement "space possesses sound," where three cognitions arise rapidly; so too it is in the arising of the cognition of duality and so forth—thus there is no fault.
If it be thought that the same fault applies even to the position of the "slayer and the slain" (*badhyaghātaka*), then it might be argued as follows:

[Objection: "In that case, even under the theory of the 'slayer and the slain' (*badhyaghātaka*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the cognition of the substance does not arise.
How so?
Because at the same time as the cognition of the generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānya*), the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is destroyed by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*). [Response: No."

Because the cognition of a collection (*samūhajñāna*) is the cause of the formative impression (*saṃskāra*), it is the cognition of the collection itself that is the cause of the impression, not the initial sensory perception (*ālocanajñāna*); thus, there is no fault.

If it is argued that this leads to the consequence of simultaneous cognitions (*jñānayaugapadyaprasaṅga*), thinking: "Surely, when cognitions are in a relationship of mutual destruction (*badhyaghātakavirodha*), the consequence of simultaneity follows," we say:
No, because we deny the persistence of two [cognitions] while they remain undestroyed.

Pdhs_8.6(113): By the statement regarding the non-simultaneity of cognitions (*jñāna*), the simultaneous arising of two cognitions and the simultaneous persistence of two [cognitions] that have not yet perished are negated. For there is no simultaneous arising of two cognitions in a relationship of mutual destruction, nor is there simultaneous persistence of two [cognitions] that are perishing. Pdhs_8.7(130.20-): Dimension (*parimāṇa*) is the cause for the conventional usage of measurement. It is fourfold: minute (*aṇu*), large (*mahat*), long (*dīrgha*), and short (*hrasva*).
In that regard, the great (mahat) is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal.

Eternal [greatness] is the supreme magnitude found in space, time, direction, and the self; non-eternal [greatness] exists only in triads (tryaṇuka) and so forth. Likewise, the minute (aṇu) is also of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal.
In eternal atoms and minds, that [dimension] is spherical (pārimāṇḍalya).
It is non-eternal only in the dyad (dvyaṇuka).

Even in large objects such as the water-lily, the myrobalan, and the bilva fruit, the conventional usage of "atomic" (aṇutva) is figurative, depending on the presence or absence of the excellence of that [spherical dimension].
Length and shortness are produced [as qualities] inhering in the same substrate as largeness and minuteness.

Even in things such as sacrificial fuel-sticks, sugarcane, and bamboo, which are directly long, the conventional usage of "shortness" is figurative, depending on the presence or absence of that excellence [of length].
Furthermore, all four types of non-eternal dimension originate from number, magnitude, and aggregation.

In that regard, the number "plurality" (*bahutvasaṃkhyā*), which has arisen in dependence upon the cognition of a lord (*īśvara*) with respect to the dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*), produces both largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) simultaneously with the production of color and other qualities in the effect-substance characterized as a triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, which is initiated by those [dyads].
However, in an effect-substance initiated by two or many large [substances], it is only the largenesses of the causes that initiate largeness, not plurality;
for even when initiated by substances of equal number, a difference in degree is observed.

In a double-cotton-fiber (*dvitūlaka*), magnitude (*mahattva*) is initiated by two balls of cotton (*pracaya-tūlapiṇḍa*) currently existing, depending either on the loose conjunctions of the constituent parts that initiate the balls, or on the mutual conjunctions of the parts of the balls; it does not arise from plurality (*bahutva*) or [other] magnitudes.
This is because an excellence is observed in what is produced by [balls] having an equal number and weight (*pala*).
Furthermore, the number two (*dvitvasaṃkhyā*) residing in two atoms initiates minuteness (*aṇutva*) in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).

Just as largeness [arises], length arises in the triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth from the multiplicity of causes, from largeness, and from homogeneous accumulation (*pracaya*). Just as minuteness [arises] in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), shortness arises from the number two.
Now, what is the distinction between largeness and length as they exist in the triad and so forth, and between minuteness and shortness as they exist in the dyads?

In that regard, there is a mutual distinction between largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*), because we observe specific conventional usage such as, "Let the long one be brought from among the large," and "Let the large one be brought from among the long.
However, the mutual distinction between minuteness (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*) is perceptible to those who perceive them.
Furthermore, all four types of dimension, being produced, perish solely through the destruction of their substratum.
Distinctness (pṛthaktva) is the cause for the linguistic usage of separation and differentiation.
Furthermore, it resides in a single substance as well as in multiple substances.
Its eternity, non-eternity, and production are explained by [the same rules as] those of number (saṃkhyā).

However, this is the distinction: just as with oneness and so forth, there is an absence of further universals (aparasāmānya) in respect to single separateness and the like; yet they are distinguished by number, because we observe linguistic usage qualified by that [number].
Conjunction (*samyoga*) is the cause of the cognition of "conjoined.
It is also the cause of substances, qualities, and actions.

Regarding the initiation of a substance, it functions as such when independent; this is because of the statement: "[A substance arises] from those that are dependent and from those that are independent."
However, in the commencement of qualities and actions, it is dependent [on other factors], because of the Vaiśeṣika statement: "The specific quality of fire [arises] from conjunction.
Now, what are its characteristics and how many kinds are there?

Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the reaching together of two things that were previously unjoined; and it is of three kinds: produced by the action of one, produced by the action of both, and produced by another conjunction.
Among these, that produced by the action of one [of two bodies] occurs when a moving body [acts upon] a stationary one,

as in the case of a hawk [striking] a post, or of all-pervading entities [acting upon] material objects. That produced by the action of both occurs through the collision of two bodies with opposing directional movements.
Just as in the case of two wrestlers or two rams.

Conjunction produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja*) is a conjunction occurring between an effect and a non-cause, preceded by a conjunction between a cause and a non-cause; it belongs to that which has just arisen or that which has long since arisen, and which is currently devoid of motion.
It arises from one, from two, or from many.
First, from the conjunction of one yarn and one *vīraṇa* grass stalk, there arises the conjunction of two yarns with one *vīraṇa* stalk.
From two conjunctions of a yarn with space, there arises one conjunction of two yarns with space.
And from many conjunctions of yarns with a shuttle, there arises one conjunction of a cloth with a shuttle.
And the production of two from one:
how so?

When there is a conjunction of an earth atom and a water atom, and simultaneously another conjunction occurs—of the earth atom with another earth atom and of the water atom with another water atom—then by those two conjunctions, two dyads (dvyaṇuka), one of earth and one of water, are produced simultaneously.

Pdhs_8.9(140) Then, at the very time when color and other qualities arise in the two dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) through the sequence beginning with the qualities of their causes, at that same time, from the conjunction existing between the mutual cause and the non-cause, two conjunctions existing between the mutual effect and the non-effect arise simultaneously.
What is the reason?

For it is a logical principle (*nyāya*) that an effect must necessarily be conjoined with the non-cause that is conjoined with its own cause. Therefore, the earth dyad is conjoined with the water atom which is conjoined with its own cause; likewise, the water dyad is conjoined with the earth atom which is conjoined with its own cause.
Now, how is there a mutual connection between two dyads that are connected to their respective causes and non-causes?
Their connection is also through two conjunctions produced by conjunction.
There is no unproduced conjunction, because it is not mentioned separately, like the eternal spherical dimension (*parimaṇḍala*).

Just as, after stating that the four kinds of dimension (*parimāṇa*) are produced, [the author] says "the spherical is eternal" (*nityaṃ parimaṇḍalam*), so too, after stating that conjunctions such as those produced by the action of one of two things (*anyatarakarmaja*) are produced, he would have to declare them separately to be eternal; however, he did not say so. Therefore, there is no eternal conjunction. The conjunction of space and the other [all-pervading substances] with atoms is a partial conjunction (*pradeśavṛtti*) produced by the action of one of the two. However, there is no mutual conjunction among all-pervading substances (*vibhu*) because they lack separable existence (*yutasiddhi*).

Furthermore, that [conjunction] consists in either both or one of two things having separate motion or having separate substrata and superstrata. Destruction, however, occurs for every conjunction either from disjunction inhering in the same object [as the conjunction], or in some cases, also from the destruction of the substratum. How so?

When there is a conjunction of two threads, an action arises in one of the constituent parts (*aṃśu*) that initiates the thread. By that action, a disjunction is produced from the other part; from that disjunction, the destruction of the conjunction that initiated the thread occurs; from the destruction of that conjunction, the destruction of the thread follows; and upon its destruction, the destruction of the conjunction with the other thread—which was dependent upon it—occurs. Disjunction is the cause of the cognition of "separatedness" and is also the cause of the production of sound.
Disjunction (*vibhāga*) is the non-attainment (*aprāpti*) that follows upon attainment (*prāpti*).
It is of three kinds:
disjunction produced by the action of one [of two bodies], disjunction produced by the action of both, and disjunction produced by [a prior] disjunction.
In this regard, [disjunction] produced by the action of one [of two things], or produced by the actions of both, is like conjunction.

However, that produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja*) is of two kinds: from the disjunction of causes and from the disjunction of cause and non-cause. Regarding the first, concerning disjunction from the cause: when an action has arisen in a cause that is occupied by its effect, it produces a disjunction from another part of that [cause], but not yet from a location such as space; and when it produces a disjunction from a location such as space, it does not [yet] produce a disjunction from another part—such is the established rule.

From this [action], the action of a part initiates a disjunction from another part; from that disjunction, there is the destruction of the conjunction that originates the substance. When that [conjunction] has been destroyed, due to the absence of its cause, there is the absence of its effect—thus, the composite whole is destroyed. At that time, the disjunction residing in the two causes, depending on the time characterized by the destruction of the effect, or depending on the independent part itself, initiates a disjunction of the active part alone from a location such as space that was conjoined with the effect; it does not do so for the inactive part, because of the absence of a cause, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of that part being unenjoyable due to the non-production of a subsequent conjunction. However, that action of the part does indeed produce a conjunction with another location, because there is no lapse of time for an action that has not yet produced its conjunction.
How [is it] also from the division of the cause and the non-cause?

When an action produced in the hand, without effecting a division from another part, initiates divisions from locations such as space and then initiates conjunctions in another location, then those divisions of the cause and the non-cause—relative to that direction toward which the action is oriented for the commencement of the effect—initiate divisions of the effect and the non-effect. Immediately after that, from the conjunction of the cause and the non-cause, there arise conjunctions of the effect and the non-effect.

If it is argued that "if the production of the disjunction of the effect follows immediately after the disjunction of the cause, and the production of the conjunction of the effect follows immediately after the conjunction of the cause, then does this not entail the fault of the parts and the whole being established separately (*yutasiddhi*)?", we say: no. This is because there is a lack of understanding regarding what constitutes separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*). Furthermore, that [separate establishment] consists in either both or one of two things possessing distinct motion. However, for eternal things, it is inherent existence (*samavāya*); whereas for non-eternal things, separate establishment is inherence in separate substrata.

In the case of the tactile faculty (*tvagindriya*) and the body, there is no possession of separate motion; since they possess inherence (*samavāya*) in their respective substrates, their mutual conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is established.
However, in the case of an atom (*aṇu*) and space (*ākāśa*), even though there is no other substrate, conjunction and disjunction are established because one of the two possesses separate motion.
As for the thread and the cloth, which are impermanent, since there is no other substrate, there is an absence of conjunction and disjunction with respect to each other.
However, because the directions and so forth lack separate motion, there is no mutual conjunction or disjunction between them.

As for the destruction [of disjunction], since every disjunction is momentary and exists only until the occurrence of a subsequent conjunction, it is momentary. But disjunction does not belong to conjunction and cognition alone, nor is its destruction caused by the conjunction of those two. Why? Because, unlike the cognition of conjunction, there is no persistence of a cognition of disjunction; therefore, because it exists only until the occurrence of a subsequent conjunction, it is momentary.

In some cases, it perishes simply through the destruction of its substratum. How so? When an action has arisen in a constituent part (*aṃśu*) which is a causal factor of a two-threaded fabric (*dvitantuka*), and it initiates a disjunction from another constituent part, at that very same time an action arises in the other thread as well. Through that disjunction, the conjunction that originated the thread is destroyed; simultaneously, a disjunction from the other thread is produced by the action of the [first] thread. Thus, these occur at one and the same time.

Then, at the very moment when the destruction of the conjunction of the threads occurs due to disjunction, at that same moment, the destruction of the threads occurs due to the destruction of the conjunction; and when that [conjunction] has perished, there is the destruction of the disjunction from the other thread which was dependent upon it.
If this were so, it would follow that no subsequent disjunction could arise, because of the absence of a disjunction of the cause.

Consequently, because there is an absence of conjunction in that which possesses conjunction with another location, action would persist for a long duration due to the impossibility of a contrary quality; furthermore, that which inheres in an eternal substance would itself be eternal—this is the fault. How so?

When an action has arisen in a primary atom that is about to initiate a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), it simultaneously produces a disjunction from another atom; at that very same time, an action also arises in that other atom. Then, at the same moment that the conjunction initiating the substance is destroyed by that disjunction, a disjunction between the dyad and the [other] atom is produced by the action in the other atom. Then, at the same moment that the conjunction of the dyad and the atom is destroyed by that disjunction, the dyad itself is destroyed due to the destruction of its conjunction.

When that [conjunction] has perished, there is the destruction of the disjunction of the dyad from its atom which was dependent upon it; and consequently, because of the impossibility of a contrary quality, action inherent in an eternal substance would be eternal.
[To this we reply: There is no fault, for there is a further disjunction resulting from the disjunction of the thread from another part.

Because the substratum is destroyed, the disjunction from the thread itself is destroyed, but the disjunction from the other parts of the thread is not; from this, a subsequent disjunction arises, just as there is a disjunction of the body from space resulting from the disjunction of a finger from space. At that very same time, the action, having produced the conjunction, perishes; thus, there is no fault.

Alternatively, at the same time that the disjunction from another part arises, an action is produced in that very thread. Then, from the disjunction from the other part, there is the destruction of the conjunction that originated the thread; and by the action of the thread, a disjunction from the other thread is produced—this constitutes one moment of time.

Thereafter, from the destruction of the conjunction, there is the destruction of the thread; and from its destruction, there is the simultaneous destruction of the disjunction and the action which were dependent upon it.

Or, when there is a conjunction between a thread and vīraṇa grass, since no new substance is produced, the destruction of the disjunction between the thread and the vīraṇa grass occurs through the previously mentioned method, namely by means of the destruction of the substratum and the [original] conjunction.
Remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) are the causes for the designations and cognitions of "remote" and "proximate.
These are of two kinds: produced by space (*dikkṛta*) and produced by time (*kālakṛta*).
Among these, that produced by space is what brings about the cognition of a particular direction.
That which is produced by time (kālakṛta) indicates a difference in age.
Among those, the production of that which is produced by space (dikkṛta) is now explained.
How so?

When two objects situated in the same direction possess a greater or lesser degree of conjunction with the points of space, for a single observer, having taken one as the proximate limit, there arises in the substratum of "priority" (the more distant object) a cognition of it being "distant," such that "this is further than that.
Then, depending upon that [cognition], priority arises from the conjunction with a more remote spatial region.
Likewise, having taken the distant object as the limit, there arises in the other—the substratum of "posteriority"—a cognition of it being "proximate," such that "this is nearer than that."
Then, through conjunction with another spatial direction in relation to that [first object], the production of "posteriority" occurs.
How does it occur for those produced by time?

When two people—a youth and an elder—both existing in the present time and conjoined with indeterminate spatial directions, are present together with such features as a grown beard, roughness, wrinkles, and gray hair, a certain observer, taking the youth as the limit (*avadhi*), produces a cognition of remoteness regarding the elder.
Then, depending on that [prior cognition], through conjunction with a subsequent spatial-temporal point, the production of "remoteness" (*paratva*) occurs.
Furthermore, taking the elder as the limit (*avadhi*), a cognition of proximity arises regarding the youth;
then, depending on that [cognition], through conjunction with a subsequent spatial-temporal point, the production of "nearness" (*aparatva*) occurs.

Destruction, however, results from the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), the conjunction, and the substance. First, regarding destruction by the destruction of the relative cognition: at the time when, after distance (*paratva*) has arisen, the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) arises, then there is the state of the relative cognition being about to perish; and simultaneously with the knowledge of the universal and its relation [to the substance], there is the arising of the cognition of the quality of distance (*paratvaguṇabuddhi*). These constitute one single moment.

Then, from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), there is the arising of the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*). Then, from the destruction of the enumerative cognition, there is the state of the quality being about to perish; and from the cognition of the quality, its relation [to the substance], and so forth, there is the arising of the cognition of the substance (*dravyabuddhi*)—this is one moment. Then, from the arising of the cognition of the substance, there is the destruction of the quality.
How also [does it occur] from the destruction of the conjunction (*saṃyogavināśa*)?

Simultaneously with the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), an action arises in the substratum of "priority" (*paratva*). By that action, a disjunction from the spatial point (*dikpiṇḍa*) is produced; and from the relative cognition, the production of priority occurs—this constitutes one moment. Thereafter, there is the production of the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) and the destruction of the conjunction between the spatial point and the object. Then, at the very moment when the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*) arises, the destruction of the quality occurs due to the destruction of the conjunction between the spatial point and the object.
How [does it occur] also through the destruction of the substance (*dravya*)?

When action arises in a constituent part that serves as the substratum for "otherness" (*paratva*), at the very same time that it produces disjunction from another constituent part, the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises. Then, at the very same time that the destruction of the conjunction [of the whole] occurs due to that disjunction, "otherness" arises. Subsequently, from the destruction of the conjunction comes the destruction of the substance; and from its destruction comes the destruction of the quality (*guṇa*) that depends upon it. How, then, can there be simultaneous destruction of both the substance and the relative cognition?

When action arises in a constituent part that serves as the substratum for "remoteness" (*paratva*), at that very same time, the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises; by means of that action, a disjunction from another constituent part is produced, and the production of "remoteness" occurs—this is one moment.

Then, at the very same time that the destruction of the conjunction initiating the substance [the whole] occurs due to the disjunction of the parts, at that same time, the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) arises; immediately thereafter, the destruction of the substance occurs due to the destruction of the conjunction, and the destruction of the relative cognition occurs due to the cognition of the universal—this is one moment.
Then, due to the destruction of the cognition of relative distance (*apekṣābuddhi*) which depends upon the substance, there is the destruction of "remoteness" (*paratva*).
How [does this happen] also through the destruction of the conjunction with the substance?

When an action has arisen in a part of the substratum of remoteness and produces a disjunction from another part, at that very same time, the action of the whole (*piṇḍakarman*) and the cognition of relative distance arise simultaneously. Then, at the very moment that "remoteness" arises, at that same moment, the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance occurs due to the disjunction, and a disjunction between the whole and space is produced by the action of the whole; thus, it is a single moment.

Then, at the very moment that the cognition of generality (*sāmānyabuddhi*) arises, at that same moment, due to the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance, there is the destruction of the aggregate (*piṇḍa*); and from the destruction of the aggregate, there is the destruction of the conjunction with the aggregate. Subsequently, simultaneously with the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*), due to the destruction of the aggregate, of space, and of the conjunction with the aggregate, there is the destruction of "remoteness" (*paratva*). How [is this] also [possible] through the simultaneous destruction of the conjunction and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)?

When remoteness (*paratva*) arises, there is then action (*karman*) in the substratum of that remoteness. At the very same time that the cognition of the generality (*sāmānya*) of remoteness arises, the disjunction (*vibhāga*) from the spatial point (*dikpiṇḍa*) is produced by the action of the object. Thereafter, at one and the same time, the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) occurs due to the cognition of the generality, and the destruction of the conjunction with the spatial point occurs due to the disjunction. Then, from the destruction of that conjunction and the relative cognition, follows the destruction of the remoteness itself.
How [is it] also from the simultaneous destruction of the three causes—the inherent, the non-inherent, and the efficient?

When the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises, at that same time there is motion in the constituent part of the aggregate; then, at the very moment that the motion effects a separation from another constituent part, and the relative cognition produces "priority" (*paratva*), at that same moment there is also motion in the aggregate. Then, from the separation of the parts, the conjunction that originated the aggregate is destroyed; and by the motion in the aggregate, a separation from the spatial direction (*dik*) is produced, as well as the arising of the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*). Thus, all this occurs at one and the same time.

Pdhs_8.11(167): Thereafter, from the destruction of the conjunction [of the self and the mind], there is the destruction of the aggregate; from the disjunction, there is the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the aggregate; and from the cognition of the universal [of "priority"], there is the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). Thus, all this occurs simultaneously through the destruction of the three causes—the inherent (*samavāyi*), the non-inherent (*asamavāyi*), and the efficient (*nimitta*)—which results in the destruction of "priority" (*paratva*). Pdhs_8.12(171.16): Cognition (*buddhi*), apprehension (*upalabdhi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and conceptualization (*pratyaya*) are synonyms.
And that [consciousness] has many modes because of the infinity of objects and because it is determined with respect to each individual object.
Although that [cognition] is of many kinds, it is briefly of two types: knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Among these, ignorance is fourfold, characterized by doubt, error, non-determination, and dreaming.

First, doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a deliberation that rests upon two possibilities, characterized by the thought "What could it be? arising from the perception of mere similarity between two well-known particulars, the recollection of both their specific qualities, and unwholesome karma (*adharma*).
It is of two kinds: internal and external.

Internal doubt occurs, for example, when a guide points out something and then indicates it again; at that time, a doubt arises regarding the three periods of time as to whether his indication is correct or false.

External [doubt] is of two kinds: regarding an object of perception and regarding an object beyond perception. Among these, first, regarding an object beyond perception, doubt arises from the observation of a common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-liṅga*), the recollection of both specific features, and [the influence of] demerit (*adharma*). For example, upon seeing only a horn in a forest, one wonders whether it is a cow or a gavaya.

Pdhs_8.12.1.1 Even regarding an object that is not within the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), when one perceives only the similarity of height in a post (*sthāṇu*) and a person (*puruṣa*), and because specific features such as curvature are not perceived, the particularities of the common characteristics (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) such as "post-ness" remain unmanifest. Consequently, due to the recollection of the specific features of both, the cognition of the self (*ātman*), being drawn toward both possibilities, wavers: "Is this indeed a post, or is it a person?
Pdhs_8.12.1.2 Error (*viparyaya*) also occurs only with respect to objects of direct perception or inference.

First, regarding the domain of perception (*pratyakṣa*): when the senses are impaired by bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*kapha*), or wind (*anila*), there arises from the contact of the self and the mind—dependent on a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a cognition of an object not present, and from demerit (*adharma*)—the erroneous cognition (*viparyaya*) that "this is that" with respect to what is not that.
For example, [perceiving] a cow as a horse.

Even in the absence of perception, there occurs the conceit of perception (*pratyakṣābhimāna*), such as [thinking] of the nocturnal darkness—which is like the sky over an ocean free from clouds and is dark as a heap of powdered collyrium—as being [actually perceived].

Even regarding the object of inference, there is erroneous cognition (*viparyaya*) when one infers fire from what is mistaken for smoke—such as steam—and when one perceives a cow because of seeing the horns of a *gavaya*. Furthermore, it is erroneous cognition to hold the view that the teachings of the Śākyas and others—which contradict the vision of the Three Vedas (*trayī-darśana*)—are the supreme good. It is also erroneous cognition to have the conceit of self (*ātma-abhimāna*) with respect to the body, the senses, and the mind; to perceive permanence in things that are produced; to know that an effect arises despite a deficiency in its causes; to know something as beneficial when it is taught as harmful; and to know something as harmful when it is taught as beneficial.
Non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) also arises only with respect to the objects of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).

Among these, regarding the object of perception first: non-determination is merely a state of wondering, "What is this? due to distraction or lack of interest, whether the object is well-known or unknown.
For example, a person from the Vāhīka region may experience non-determination when confronted with fruits such as the *panasa*.

In that regard, there arises a determinate cognition (*adhyavasāya*) based on existence, substantiality, earthness, treeness, possession of form, and so forth, as well as the branches and other parts. Furthermore, "jackfruit-ness" (*panasatva*), which is inclusive of jackfruit trees and exclusive of mangoes and others, is indeed directly perceived; however, due to the absence of instruction, the comprehension of its specific name does not occur.

Even regarding an object of inference, for an inhabitant of Nārikela Island, upon seeing only a dewlap, there arises a non-determinate cognition (*anadhyavasāya*) such as, "What kind of living being might this be?"
When the collection of sense-faculties has ceased and the mind has dissolved, that mental experience which occurs precisely through the doors of the sense-faculties is dream-cognition. How so?

When, due to the bodily activity of a self preceded by conscious intention, beings who are exhausted during the day rest at night for the sake of repose or for the digestion of food, then—depending on the effort induced by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and arising from the connection between the self and the internal organ—the mind remains motionless within the heart, in a region of the self that is devoid of the senses, through a continuous stream of mental activity; at that time, it is designated as "one whose mind is dissolved" (*pralīnamanaska*).

When that [dreamless sleep] has dissolved, the collection of sense-faculties comes to rest. In that state, while the continuous flow of the series of inhalation and exhalation proceeds due to a specific conjunction of the self and the mind, dream-cognition arises through the gateway of the sense-faculties—even though the objects are not present—taking the form of direct perception (*pratyakṣākāra*), owing to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) known as sleep.
That [dream-cognition] is of three kinds:
from the intensity of latent impressions, from an imbalance of the bodily humors (*dhātudoṣa*), and from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

In that regard, first, due to the proficiency of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), when one who is lustful or angry falls asleep while contemplating a certain object, that very stream of thought arises in the form of a direct perception.
Or, due to a disorder of the elements—such as one of a windy temperament (*vātaprakṛti*) or one afflicted by wind—one sees things such as traveling through the sky.
One of a bilious temperament (*pittaprakṛti*) or one afflicted by bile sees things such as entering fire or mountains of gold.
One of a phlegmatic constitution (*śleṣmaprakṛti*), or one whose phlegm is deranged (*śleṣmadūṣita*), sees rivers, oceans to be crossed, snowy mountains, and so forth.

Whatever indicates auspiciousness—whether regarding things personally experienced or not experienced, or things well-known or unknown—such as mounting an elephant, obtaining a parasol, and so on, all that arises from both merit (*dharma*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*). Conversely, whatever indicates the opposite—such as being anointed with oil, mounting a donkey or a camel, and so on—all that arises from demerit (*adharma*) and mental formations.
Regarding objects that are entirely unknown, [cognition] arises solely from what has not been seen before.

Although dream-cognition occurs when the collection of sense-faculties has ceased, it is nonetheless merely memory because it consists in the reviewing of a past continuum of cognitions. Thus, this ignorance is of four kinds.
Knowledge is also fourfold,
characterized by perception, inference, recollection, and the vision of the seers (ārṣa).
That which arises in dependence [is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)].
The sense-faculties (*akṣa*) are the six faculties: the nose, tongue, eye, body, ear, and mind.
For that [perception] arises with respect to categories of objects such as substances (*dravya*).

First, regarding substance: when it is large, possesses multiple constituent substances, and has manifested color and light, and when there is the fourfold contact [of the object with the sense organ, the sense organ with the mind, the mind with the self, and the self with the internal organ], as well as the causal complex consisting of merit (*dharma*) and so forth, there arises a mere observation of its own form.

Then, through the contact of the self and the mind, depending upon the qualifiers of generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*), perception (*pratyakṣa*) arises in the form: "It exists," "It is a substance," "It is earth," "It has horns," "It is white," "It is a cow," or "It is moving."

Perception of color, taste, odor, and touch arises through the conjunction of multiple substances, their own specific qualities, and contact with their own substrates; it is produced by means of specific sense organs, and perception occurs through those very same [organs].

Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, viscidity, fluidity, speed, and action are perceived by both the eye and the sense of touch due to their inherence in perceptible substances.
Perception (*upalabdhi*) of cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort arises from the conjunction of two [factors]: the self (*ātman*) and the mind (*manas*).

The apprehension of existence, substantiality, quality-ness, action-ness, and so forth—which are inherent in the substratum that serves as the locus of perception—by means of the sense organs that apprehend their supports, constitutes the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of persons such as ourselves.

But for yogins superior to us who are in a state of meditative union (*yukta*), through a mind aided by the dharma born of yoga, there arises an unerring perception of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) regarding their own self, other selves, ether, space, time, atoms, air, and minds, as well as the qualities, actions, universals, and particulars inherent in them, and inherence itself.

Furthermore, for those who are not in a state of union (*viyukta*), direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of subtle, concealed, or distant objects arises through the contact of the four factors, by virtue of the power of the assistance provided by the dharma born of yoga.

In that regard, with respect to universals and particulars, perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists merely in the observation of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). The objects of cognition (*prameya*) are the categories (*padārtha*) such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth. The result of the means of cognition (*pramiti*) is the knowledge whose object is substance and the other categories.

When the knowledge of universals and particulars arises, perception as a means of valid cognition is merely an undifferentiated observation; there is no other distinct means of valid cognition in this case, because [any such distinction] would lack the nature of a fruit (*phala*).

Alternatively, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which arises with respect to all objects (*padārtha*) from the fourfold contact; it is non-erroneous and non-verbal. The objects of cognition (*prameya*) are the categories (*padārtha*) such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth. The cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is the self (*ātman*). The result of cognition (*pramiti*) is the observation of qualities (*guṇa*), defects (*doṣa*), or neutrality (*mādhyasthya*). Inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika*) is that which arises from the observation of a mark (*liṅga*).
Furthermore, the logical mark (*liṅga*) is that which is related to the object to be inferred, is well-known to exist in what is similar to it,
and absolutely does not exist in its absence; such is the mark that brings about inference.
The opposite of this— whether it be [a reason] consisting of one or two [of these defects]—
Kāśyapa declared to be a non-reason (*aliṅga*), being contradictory, unestablished, or doubtful.

That which is concomitant with the object to be inferred (anumeya) in a specific place or time, which is well-known (*prasiddha*) in all or some other instance possessing the property to be inferred, and which is known through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) to be absolutely non-existent in every case contrary to the object to be inferred—that becomes the logical mark (*liṅga*) that makes the unestablished object known.
As for the positive rule (*vidhi*), it is: "Where there is smoke, there is fire; in the absence of fire, smoke does not exist."

Thus, for one who has mastered the convention [of the relationship between signs], from the perception of smoke that is free from doubt and from the recollection of its concomitance, there subsequently arises the certain determination (*adhyavasāya*) of fire.
In this way, in all cases, that which is inseparable from a particular place or time is the mark (*liṅga*) of the other.
In the treatise, the mention of "effects" and so forth was made for the sake of illustration, not for the sake of restriction; why? Because light is perceived from a single observation.

For example: the *adhvaryu* priest signaling with "Oṃ śrāvaya" is the mark of the *hotṛ* priest who is out of sight; the rising of the moon is the mark of the swelling of the ocean and the blooming of the night-lotuses; and the clarity of the water in autumn is the mark of the rising of the star Agastya.
All such cases are established by the mere statement of a relationship, namely, "this belongs to that.
Furthermore, that [relationship] is of two kinds.
[Inference is] of two kinds: that based on what has been seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and that based on what has been seen in general (*sāmānyato-dṛṣ�ṭa*).
Among these, *dṛṣṭa* is inference when there is no absolute difference in genus between the established [reason] and the probandum (*sādhya*).
For example, having perceived nothing more than a dewlap in a cow, one recognizes it as a cow upon seeing nothing more than a dewlap in another place.

Inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭam anumānam*) occurs when there is an absolute difference in genus between the well-known instance (*prasiddha*) and the object to be proven (*sādhya*), and it proceeds from the persistence of a commonality of properties between the mark (*liṅga*) and the property to be inferred (*anumeya-dharma*).

For example, having observed that the activities of farmers, merchants, and royal servants are productive of results, one infers a result for those belonging to the [four] castes and [four] stages of life (*varṇāśramin*) who act even without aiming at a visible purpose.
In this case, the perception of the mark (*liṅgadarśana*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the resulting cognition of fire (*agnijñāna*) is the valid knowledge (*pramiti*).

Alternatively, the cognition of fire itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while the perception of its qualities, defects, or neutrality regarding that fire is the resulting cognition (*pramiti*). This is inference whose object is ascertained by oneself.
Since they function according to the same principle, verbal testimony (*śabda*) and the other means of knowledge are also included within inference.

Just as inference occurs with respect to an object beyond the senses through the observation of an unmistakable mark and the recollection of its established relationship for one who has mastered the convention, so too does it occur through words and the like.

Even the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), characterized by the *śruti* and *smṛti*, depends upon the authority of its speaker; for the authority of the sacred tradition arises from his word. Furthermore, it is impermanent because the composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by intelligence, as it has been stated that "the act of giving is preceded by intelligence."
Since comprehension is observed through the gestures of one who is proficient in conventional expression, that too is indeed inference.
Because an authoritative person conveys the cognition of a gavaya, which is not previously known, by means of a cow, analogy is nothing other than the word of an authoritative person (*āptavacana*).
From the perception of one object, there is the presumption of another; from hearing what is contradictory, there is inference based on an inference.
Co-occurrence (*sambhava*) is also nothing but inference, because it is characterized by invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*).
Non-existence, too, is indeed inference: just as an effect that has arisen is a mark for the existence of its cause, so an effect that has not arisen is a mark for the non-existence of its cause.
In the same way, tradition (*aitihya*) that is unerring is also simply the instruction of a reliable person (*āptopadeśa*).
Inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is the demonstration of an object ascertained by oneself through a five-membered statement.

It should be understood that inference for the sake of others is the demonstration of an object ascertained by oneself to others—those who are doubtful, mistaken, or ignorant—exclusively by means of a five-membered statement.

Furthermore, the members [of a syllogism] are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the statement of the reason (*apadeśa*), the example (*nidarśana*), the application (*anusandhāna*), and the conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*).
Among these, the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the enunciation of the object of inference (*anumeya*) that is not contradictory [to other means of valid cognition].
The proposition is the mere enunciation intended to bring the subject (*dharmin*), as qualified by the property (*dharma*) one wishes to demonstrate, within the scope of the statement.
"For example: 'Air is a substance' (yathā dravyaṃ vāyuḥ).
By the inclusion of the term "non-contradictory" (*avirodhi*), those [theses] that contradict perception, inference, accepted scripture, one's own treatise, or one's own words are excluded.

For instance: "Fire is not hot" contradicts perception; "The sky is solid" contradicts inference; "Liquor may be drunk by a Brahmin" contradicts scripture; for a Vaiśeṣika who asserts "the effect exists [in the cause]" (*satkāryam*), it contradicts his own treatise; and "A word does not convey meaning" contradicts one's own statement.
The statement of the mark (*liṅga*) is the *apadeśa* (probans).

That which is concomitant with the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), which is established by its general presence throughout all members of the same class (*samānajātīya*), and which is entirely absent in everything contrary to it—that is called the mark. The statement of that [mark] is the *apadeśa*. For example: "Because of possessing action (*kriyāvattva*) and because of possessing quality (*guṇavattva*). And thus, these two exist in the object to be inferred; possession of quality exists in all members of the same class, while possession of action exists in some, but not in all.
Both of these [characteristics] do not exist at all in that which is non-substantial; therefore, it is established that its verbal designation is merely a figurative description (*apadeśa*).

By this, it is stated that statements which are unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), doubtful (*sandigdha*), or non-conclusive (*anadhyavasita*) do not constitute valid reasons (*anapadeśatva*).
Among these, the unestablished reason is of four kinds:

unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*), unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*), unestablished in its existence (*tadbhāvāsiddha*), and unestablished regarding the object of inference (*anumeyāsiddha*).
Among these, the unestablished for both (*ubhayāsiddha*) is that which is not established for both the proponent and the opponent, such as: "Sound is impermanent because it possesses parts.
The unestablished for one of the two (*anyatarāsiddha*) is, for example: "Sound is impermanent because it is a product.

The unestablished in its existence (*tadbhāvāsiddha*) is, for example, when steam is put forward as smoke in order to establish fire by means of the presence of smoke; in this case, the [steam] is unestablished as being smoke.

Pdhs_8.12.2.2.B.2(238) 2.2. The unestablished due to the [subject] being non-existent in the inferable (*anumeyāsiddha*): for example, "Darkness is an earth-substance because it possesses a black color.

That which, though not existing in the inferable, does not exist in anything of its own kind (*tatsamānajātīya*) but does exist in its opposite (*tadviparīta*), is "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite; for example, "Because it has horns, therefore it is a horse.

However, that which exists in the inferable but is common (*sādhāraṇa*) to both its similar and dissimilar kinds, being thus uncertain, is "doubtful" (*sandigdha*) because it generates doubt; for example, "Because it has horns, therefore it is a cow."

Some maintain that when there is a conjunction of two contradictory reasons possessing the characteristics already described, this is another type of "doubtful" (*saṃdigdha*) reason, because it gives rise to uncertainty;
