for example, with respect to whether the mind is corporeal or incorporeal, [the reasons] being its possession of motion and its lack of tangibility.

But surely this is merely the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason, like the properties of "not being visible to the eye" and "being perceptible," since neither alternative is possible for the two combined [reasons]; therefore, we shall say that it is actually the "inconclusive" (*anadhyavasita*) reason.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in various places in the treatise (*śāstra*), the observation of two ways [of stating a matter] is pointed out as a cause of doubt? [Response: No, there is no doubt here because of the observation of a duality of objects. In the arising of doubt, the observation of a duality of objects is the cause; however, when those two are of equal strength, they would fail to produce a definitive conclusion due to their mutual contradiction, but they would not be the cause of doubt. Furthermore, those two are not of equal strength, because one of the two—the subject of inference—is sublated by scripture (*āgama*). This, however, is merely a specific type of contradiction (*viruddha-bheda*).

Furthermore, that which exists in the object of inference (anumeya) but is absent from both its similar and dissimilar classes is "unestablished for one of the two parties" (anyatarāsiddha). Because it does not serve as a cause for certain determination, it is "indeterminate" (anadhyavasita). For example: "The effect pre-exists in the cause, because it arises.
This is subsumed under the statement: "That which is unestablished is not a valid reason" (aprasiddho 'napadeśaḥ).

But is it not the case that this particularity has been stated in the treatise as a cause for doubt—on the grounds that a particularity is observed in both ways among things of the same class and among those belonging to a different category? No, because the word has a different meaning; for a particularity is observed in the word itself.

When it is said that "doubt does not arise," this [audibility] would not be a specific property (*viśeṣa*) of any one among the categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth; rather, it becomes a generality (*sāmānya*) itself. Why? Because it has been stated that a specific property is observed in two ways—both within things of the same class and within things belonging to different classes—among the various divisions of substance and so on. Otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) of doubt arising even regarding all six categories. Therefore, doubt arises solely from the cognition of a generality. The illustration (*nidarśana*) is of two kinds: by similarity (*sādharmyeṇa*) and by dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*).

In that context, the demonstration of similarity (*sādharmya-nidarśana*) is the observation of the concomitance of the general mark (*liṅga-sāmānya*) with the general object to be inferred (*anumeya-sāmānya*).
For example: "Whatever possesses activity is seen to be a substance, such as an arrow.
Furthermore, the demonstration of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-nidarśana*) is the observation of the absence of the mark in the opposite of the object to be inferred.
For example: that which is not a substance does not possess activity, just like existence (sattā).

By this, fallacious examples (*nidarśanābhāsa*) are excluded. For instance: "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal; whatever is seen to be incorporeal is eternal, such as an atom, such as karma, such as a pot, such as darkness, like space," and "whatever is a substance is seen to possess action. These are respectively: fallacious examples by similarity (*sādharmya-nidarśanābhāsa*) that are unestablished with respect to the mark (*liṅga*), the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), or both; unestablished with respect to their substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*); non-concomitant (*ananugata*); and conversely concomitant (*viparītānugata*).

Whatever is impermanent is seen to be material, such as karma, or like an atom, or like space, or like darkness, or like a jar; and that which is inactive is a non-substance. These are the fallacious examples of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-nidarśana-ābhāsa*), characterized by [the fallacies of] the mark being absent from the example, the probandum being absent from the example, both being absent from the example, the locus being unestablished, the mark being absent from the subject, and the mark being present in the opposite of the subject. In an example, there is the application and connection of the general mark, previously observed together with the generality of the probandum, to the object of inference.

The connection (*anusandhāna*) is that verbal expression by which the general characteristic of the mark (*liṅgasāmānya*), which is intended merely as a property to be inferred, whose capacity has not yet been perceived, and which was observed together with the general characteristic of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmasāmānya*) in the example, is applied to the object of inference (*anumeya*).
For instance: "Air possesses motion.
And having perceived its non-existence in the absence of the object to be inferred, one concludes: "But air is not thus devoid of motion."

The conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) for the purpose of producing certainty in others regarding that which was indicated as the object of inference and which remains unsettled.

The restatement of the proposition (*pratyāmnāya*) is the restatement of the proposition for the purpose of producing certainty in others—whose capacities have been stimulated by the other members of the syllogism, such as the reason (*hetu*), etc.—by means of a completed sentence, regarding that which was indicated as the object to be established and which remains unsettled;
[as in]: "Therefore, it is indeed a substance."

If it is argued that when this [word] is absent, other components—whether taken collectively or individually—lack the capacity to express that meaning because their meaning is already understood, we say no, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For instance, immediately after the thesis (*pratijñā*), one need only state the reason (*hetu*); since the learned possess the recollection of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the understanding of its meaning will occur. Therefore, the completion of the purpose lies in this very [statement].

"How is sound impermanent?"—by this, sound is stated as being characterized merely by the unascertained property of impermanence. "Because it follows immediately upon effort"—by this, the mere probans-property that establishes impermanence is expressed. Here, "whatever follows immediately upon effort is seen to be impermanent, like a jar"—by this, the mere concomitance of the general probans with the general probandum is stated.
"An eternal thing is observed to not be produced by effort, just like space. By this, the absence of the probans is demonstrated in the case of the absence of the property to be proven.

And thus: "Sound is observed to be produced immediately after an effort, and unlike space, sound is not produced without being preceded by an effort. By means of these positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the application (*anusandhāna*) of the general probans (*sādhana-sāmānya*), whose capacity has been observed, is understood to apply to sound; therefore, it is established that "sound is non-eternal. Through this, the completion of the intended meaning—that sound is indeed non-eternal—is understood. Consequently, it is established that inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) consists in the communication of an object ascertained by oneself through a syllogism consisting of exactly five members.

The knowledge that arises from the perception of specific characteristics (*viśeṣadarśanaja*), which consists of a definitive cognition (*avadhāraṇajñāna*) and opposes doubt (*saṃśayavirodhin*), is *nirṇaya* (ascertainment).
This very [ascertainment] is either perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).
That which arises from the perception of specific characteristics and opposes doubt is *pratyakṣanirṇaya* (perceptual ascertainment).

Just as, when doubt arises—such as "Is this a post or a person?"—due to the perception of a mere similarity in height between a post and a person, while their specific features remain unperceived, yet through the recollection of the specific features of both; and subsequently, upon seeing the head, hands, and so forth, there arises the definitive knowledge "This is indeed a person," that is *pratyakṣa-nirṇaya* (ascertainment by perception).

Similarly, when doubt arises—such as "Is this a cow or a gavaya?"—due to the sight of a mere horn, yet upon seeing a dewlap, there arises the definitive knowledge "This is indeed a cow," that is *anumāna-nirṇaya* (ascertainment by inference).

Memory is that which has past objects as its domain; it is the cause of recollection, desire, and aversion regarding things previously seen, heard, or experienced. It arises from a specific conjunction of the self and the mind dependent upon the observation of a sign, desire, and recollection, and from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by vivid perception, repeated practice, or intense interest.

The knowledge that arises from the contact of the self and the mind, due to the specific quality of merit (*dharma*), which consists of the intuitive revelation of things as they truly are—whether they pertain to the past, future, or present; whether they are beyond the senses; whether they are objects such as *dharma* and so forth; and whether they are recorded in texts or not—that is called the *ārṣa* (sage-like) [perception].
This occurs generally among the divine sages (*devarṣis*), but occasionally even among worldly people, as when a young girl says, "My brother will arrive tomorrow," or "My heart tells me so."

The vision of the perfected ones (*siddha*) is not a separate type of knowledge. Why? Because the vision of those perfected ones—such as those possessing ointments, foot-ointments, swords, or pills—who have attained the power to see visible objects that are subtle, concealed, or distant, is indeed nothing but perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, if it is claimed that there is a vision of the ripening of merit and demerit based on the signs of celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial beings, such as the conjunctions of planets and constellations, that too is merely inference (*anumāna*).

Now, if it is maintained that the perception of dharma and so forth does not depend on indicative marks (liṅga), even that is included within either perception (pratyakṣa) or authoritative testimony (ārya); thus is the cognition [to be understood].
Pleasure has the characteristic of being beneficial (*anugraha*).

When desired objects such as garlands are present, pleasure arises from the contact of the sense organs with their objects and from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on merit (*dharma*) and other factors; it is that which produces benefit, attachment, and clarity of the eyes and so forth.
That [pleasure] arising regarding past objects is born of memory.

That which arises from conceptualization regarding future objects is that which manifests for the wise even when there is no recollection, desire, or conceptualization of non-existent objects; it has as its cause specific factors such as knowledge, tranquility, contentment, and dharma.
Suffering characterized by affliction (*upaghāta-lakṣaṇa-duḥkha*):

When undesirable objects such as poison are present, suffering arises from the contact between the sense faculties and their objects, resulting in the perception of what is undesired; it is produced through the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on demerit (*adharma*) and other factors, and has the nature of indignation, affliction, and dejection.
Furthermore, it arises from the recollection of past [objects] such as snakes, tigers, and thieves.
Regarding the future, [it is] born of conceptualization. Thus.
Desire (*icchā*) is the longing for what has not yet been attained, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others.
It arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on pleasure and so forth, or depending on memory.
It is the cause of effort (*prayatna*), memory (*smṛti*), merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*).

Desire (*kāma*), longing (*abhilāṣa*), passion (*rāga*), volition (*saṅkalpa*), compassion (*kāruṇya*), detachment (*vairāgya*), hypocrisy (*upadhā*), disposition (*bhāva*), and so forth—these are the various forms of desire (*icchā*).
Desire for sexual intercourse is *kāma*;
desire for food is *abhilāṣa*.
Attachment (*rāga*) is the desire for repeated enjoyment of sense objects.
Resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is the desire for action that is not yet imminent.
Compassion (*kāruṇya*) is the desire to eliminate the suffering of others without regard for one's own interest.
Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the desire to renounce sense objects due to perceiving their defects.
Guile (*upadhā*) is the desire to deceive others. Deceit (*bhāva*) is a desire concealed within.
Differences in desire arise from differences in action, such as the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and the desire to abandon (*jihīrṣā*).

Hatred has the nature of burning. That state in which one feels as if one's very self is ablaze is hatred. It arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending either upon suffering or upon memory.
Effort, memory, dharma, and adharma are its causes.
Anger, malice, resentment, intolerance, and impatience are varieties of hatred.

Effort (*prayatna*) consists of exertion (*saṃrambha*), enthusiasm (*utsāha*), and application (*prayāya*). It is of two kinds: that preceded by vitality (*jīvana-pūrvaka*) and that preceded by desire and aversion (*icchā-dveṣa-pūrvaka*).
Among these, that preceded by vitality...
It is the impeller of the continuum of the prāṇa and apāna breaths for one who is asleep, and at the time of awakening, it is the cause of the internal organ's reaching toward other sense organs.

Its production arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, preceded by life and dependent upon merit and demerit. The other [type of effort], however, is the cause of activity capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, and it is that which sustains the body.
And that [motion] arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on desire or depending on hatred.
Gravity is the cause of the action of falling in water and earth.
It is imperceptible and is to be inferred from the action of falling. It is opposed to conjunction, effort, and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Its eternity, non-eternity, and production are like those of the color and other qualities of atoms such as fire and so forth.
Fluidity is the cause of the action of flowing. It resides in three substances. It is, moreover, of two kinds: natural and incidental.
Inherent [fluidity] is the specific quality of water;
adventitious [fluidity] is a common quality of earth and fire.
Regarding inherent fluidity, its eternity, non-eternity, and production are like those of gravity.
If it is argued that [fluidity] is not inherent (*sāṃsiddhika*) because it is observed as a result of aggregation (*saṅghāta*), we say no.

For water atoms (*āpya-paramāṇu*) conjoined with divine heat (*divya-tejas*) undergo mutual conjunction called "aggregation" (*saṅghāta*), which initiates a substance. Due to this, the fluidity of the atoms is obstructed; consequently, fluidity does not arise in the effect, such as snow or hail.
Furthermore, occasional (*naimittika*) fluidity arises from the conjunction of fire in earth and light.

How is it that in the case of ghee, lac, beeswax, and so forth, when action arises in their constituent atoms due to contact with fire depending on momentum (*vega*), then—following from the disjunctions produced by that [action]—the conjunctions that initiate the substance are destroyed, and upon the cessation of the effect-substance, fluidity (*dravatva*) arises in the independent atoms due to contact with fire depending on heat (*auṣṇya*). Subsequently, when action arises in those [atoms] due to contact between the self and the atoms depending on the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the experiencers, then—following from the conjunctions produced by that [action]—the effect-substance is produced through the process beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). And in that [substance], at the same time as the production of color and other qualities, fluidity arises through the process of the qualities of the causes.
Viscosity (*sneha*) is the specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of water (*ap*).
It is the cause of cohesion (*saṃgraha*), purification (*mṛjā*), and so forth.
Like gravity (*gurutva*), its permanence, impermanence, and production are also [to be understood] in the same way.
Impression (*saṃskāra*) is threefold: velocity (*vega*), mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*).

Among these, velocity arises from action dependent on specific causes within the five corporeal substances; it is the cause of a continuous series of movements in a fixed direction, is opposed by specific conjunctions with tangible substances, and in some cases arises through a sequence beginning with the qualities of the cause.

That which is termed mental cultivation, however, is a quality of the self; it is the cause of memory and recognition regarding objects seen, heard, or experienced, and is opposed by knowledge, intoxication, pain, and so forth.

That which is born from sharpness, repetition, and earnest application: from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon a sharp cognition regarding a marvelous object, a sharp excellence of latent impression (*saṃskārātiśaya*) arises—just as, for example, occurs for a person from the South upon seeing a camel. When learning, arts, physical exercises, and so forth are being practiced, an excellence of latent impression arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon each subsequent cognition in relation to that very same object and in dependence upon each preceding latent impression.

Having fixed the mind and the eyes with effort upon an object never before seen, for one desiring to perceive it, there arises a cognition of intense interest—like the sight of a flash of lightning. From the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon that [cognition], an excellence of latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced;
as, for example, from the sight of silver and golden lotuses in the celestial lake of the gods.

The elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*), however, residing in tangible substances that possess dense and specific configurations of parts and persist over time, restores its own substratum to its original state when it has been altered.
The function of elasticity (sthiti-sthāpaka) is observed in stationary and mobile modifications—such as bows, branches, horns, tusks, bones, threads, and cloth—when they are bent or compressed;
its properties of permanence, impermanence, and production are like those of gravity.

Dharma is a quality of the person (*puruṣaguṇa*). It is the cause of what is pleasant, beneficial, and liberation for the agent; it is supersensible (*atīndriya*); it is opposed to the consciousness of final bliss; it arises from the conjunction of the person and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) when there is a pure intention; and it has as its cause specific means prescribed for those belonging to the various castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*).

Its means, however, are substances, qualities, and actions prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* for those of the various castes and stages of life, existing in the relationship of general and particular.

In this regard, the general duties for all [classes] are: faith in the Dharma, non-violence, benevolence toward living beings, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, freedom from deceit, avoidance of anger, ritual bathing, the use of purifying substances, devotion to a specific deity, fasting, and vigilance.

For the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya, [the common duties are] sacrifice, study, and giving. The specific duties of the Brāhmaṇa are: receiving gifts, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and the sacraments prescribed for his own class. The specific duties of the Kṣatriya are: the proper protection of subjects, the suppression of the wicked, not retreating in battles, and the sacraments prescribed for his own class.
For the Vaiśya, [the duties are] trade, commerce, agriculture, cattle-rearing, and his own purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
For the Śūdra, [the duty is] dependence on the preceding varnas and performing rites without mantras.

As for those in the stages of life (*āśrama*), the student (*brahmacārin*) living in the teacher’s household has the duties prescribed by his own scripture: service to the teacher, tending the fire, gathering fuel, and the practice of begging for alms, as well as the avoidance of honey, meat, sleeping during the day, applying collyrium, anointing with oil, and so forth.

For a householder who has completed his studies and vows and has taken a wife, there is the daily performance in the morning and evening of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*)—dedicated to beings, humans, gods, ancestors, and Brahman—using wealth acquired through the *śālīna* and *yāyāvara* modes of livelihood; as well as the performance of the obligatory cooked-sacrifice rites (*pākayajñasamsthā*) according to the rules for the single fire (*ekāgni*), and, when the capacity exists, the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) and other oblation-sacrifice rites (*haviryajñasamsthā*), and the Soma-sacrifice rites (*somayajñasamsthā*) such as the *agniṣṭoma*, during the intervals between seasons; as well as celibacy and the procreation of offspring.

For one who has gone forth from the village—whether a student (*brahmacārin*) or a householder—there is dwelling in the forest, as well as wearing bark garments, skins, and maintaining the hair, beard, nails, and body hair.
For the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), there is the eating of wild forest produce and the remnants of offerings made to guests.

For the wandering mendicant (*pravrajita*), who is faithful and belongs to any of the three [preceding stages], there is the accomplishment of yoga through the constant contemplation of the six categories, having renounced his own duties after granting perpetual fearlessness to all beings and remaining vigilant in the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*).
Without aiming at any visible purpose, these means of accomplishment, depending upon clarity of disposition, result in the arising of *dharma* from the conjunction of the self and the mind.
Adharma is also a quality of the self (*ātman*).
It is the cause of harm and spiritual transgression for the agent; it is supersensible (*atīndriya*) and is opposed to the final consciousness of suffering.

Its means of accomplishment are those prohibited in the treatise (*śāstra*), which are the opposites of the means of accomplishing dharma, such as violence, falsehood, theft, and so forth, as well as the non-performance of prescribed duties and negligence. These, depending upon a corrupt intention, arise from the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃyoga*).

For one who is ignorant and possessed of passion and hatred, from a predominant virtuous action (*dharma*) accompanied by a small amount of non-virtue (*adharma*), there arises a connection with desirable bodies, sense-faculties, objects, pleasures, and so forth, in accordance with their dispositions, within the worlds of Brahmā, Indra, Prajāpati, the ancestors, and humans.

Likewise, from a predominant non-virtuous action (*adharma*) accompanied by a small amount of virtue, there arises a connection with undesirable bodies, sense-faculties, objects, and sufferings in the states of hungry ghosts and the animal realm.
Thus, from dharma characterized by such activity when conjoined with adharma, there arises the repeated bondage of saṃsāra among gods, humans, animals, and denizens of hell.

However, from an action performed preceded by knowledge and without a desire for its fruit, one is born into a pure family. Seeking the means to eliminate suffering, one approaches a teacher; having attained knowledge of the reality of the six categories, ignorance ceases. For one who is thus dispassionate, passion, hatred, and the like no longer exist. Consequently, since merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—which arise from those [passions]—do not arise, and those previously accumulated are extinguished through experience, there arises the happiness of contentment and the dissolution of the body. Upon the cessation of passion and the rest, the absolute merit characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti-lakṣaṇa*), having produced the happiness born of the vision of the ultimate truth, itself ceases.

Then, due to that cessation, there is the withdrawal of the self, mind, body, and so forth from their seeds; with the non-arising of body and so forth again, there is tranquility like a fire whose fuel is consumed—this is liberation.

Sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*); it is perceivable by the ear, momentary, and opposed by both its cause and its effect. It is produced from conjunction, disjunction, and sound; it exists in specific locations (*pradeśavṛtti*), and it has causes that are both similar and dissimilar in kind. It is of two types: characterized as phonemes (*varṇa*) and characterized as noise (*dhvani*). Among these, the phoneme-characterized consists of *a* and so forth, while the noise-characterized is caused by conch shells and the like.

In that regard, the production of what is characterized as sound (*varṇa*) arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon memory. Immediately thereafter, there is an intention to utter the sound; following that, an effort [is made]. Depending upon that effort, an action is produced in the air (*vāyu*) due to the conjunction of the self and the air. Moving upward, that [air] strikes the throat and other [articulatory organs]. Then, depending upon the conjunction of the air with those locations, sound is produced from the conjunction of the location and space (*ākāśa*).
Even that which is not characterized as sound is produced from the conjunction of the drum and the stick, depending upon the conjunction of the drum and space.

From the division of the joints of a bamboo, from the division of the space within the bamboo, and from sound produced by conjunction and disjunction, there arises a series of sounds like a succession of waves. Thus, it is through this series that sound, having reached the region of the ear, is perceived. Since there is no going or coming of either the ear or the sound, there is no perception of what has not been reached; therefore, by process of elimination, the existence of the series is established. The section on the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*) in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* is completed.
Now follows the determination of the category of action (*karma*).
Even for the five types beginning with upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), there is a connection with the nature of action.

The particularity (*viśeṣa*) consists in: possessing a single substance; momentariness; subsisting in corporeal substances; being devoid of qualities; being produced by gravity, fluidity, effort, and conjunction; being opposed to the conjunction that is its own effect; being a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction; being a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); initiating effects inherent in its own substrate and in another substrate; not initiating [effects] of the same class; not initiating [other] substances; possessing a specific genus; and initiating effects characterized by spatial direction.

Among these, upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*) is that action which, arising from gravity, effort, and conjunction, causes conjunction with upper parts and disjunction from lower parts in respect to the limbs of the body and their attachments. Downward motion (*apakṣepaṇa*) is the action that causes the opposite conjunctions and disjunctions.

When there is disjunction of the foremost parts of a straight substance from their respective locations and conjunction with its root parts by means of that action through which the whole becomes curved, that is contraction (*ākuñcana*).
Pdhs_9.2.2 (292.3): By the opposite of that [contraction], when conjunction and disjunction arise, that action by which the whole becomes straight is extension (*prasāraṇa*).
That which is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions with indefinite spatial directions is motion.

This fivefold karma—whether it pertains to the limbs of the body and their related parts, or whatever else exists with a supporting condition (*sapratyaya*) or without a supporting condition (*apratyaya*)—is merely the movement toward those [limbs] and other things; that movement itself lacks a supporting condition.
Thus, it is illogical for actions to be of five types, because there is no distinction in the nature of their movement.

For every action is momentary; having arisen as a mere movement, it produces conjunctions and disjunctions with points of space—whether upward, downward, or obliquely—by means of its own substrate through infinitesimal parts. Since the cognition of "movement" remains constant everywhere, one might conclude that everything is indeed movement. This is not so, because we observe the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to their respective classes: here there is "upward throwing," elsewhere "downward throwing," and so forth. Thus, since the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions are observed everywhere according to their classes, we understand that the cause of this is a distinction between universals and particulars.

Because they initiate specific effects distinguished by particular directions due to the specific prefixes such as *ud-* and others, a distinction in their defining characteristics (*upalakṣaṇabheda*) is also established.
Even so, the restriction that "there are exactly five" is untenable,
because even in actions such as exiting and entering, one observes the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to their respective classes.

If a distinction of universals (jāti) is desired because the persistence and exclusion of cognitions are observed in every case among throwing upwards and so forth, then the same would apply to going out, entering, and so on as well. If it is argued that the persistence and exclusion of cognitions in those [latter] cases are due to a difference in their effects, then by that same logic of difference in effects, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the persistence and exclusion of cognitions occurring even among throwing upwards and so forth. Now, if one were to say: "Even though the persistence and exclusion of cognitions in groups are equally present, there is a specific reason why a distinction of universals exists only for throwing upwards and so forth, and not for going out and so forth," we reply: no, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of a confusion of universals (jātisaṅkara).
If [the universal] were to follow or exclude based on the difference in types such as "going out" and so forth, then a confusion of universals (*jātisaṅkara*) would result.

How so? When two observers move from one room to another room simultaneously, both the cognition of "going out" and the cognition of "entering" are observed; likewise, at the doorway, there are the cognitions "he enters" and "he goes out.
However, when the curtain or other obstructions are removed, there is neither the cognition of entering nor the cognition of going out, but rather only the cognition of "moving."

Likewise, when a bamboo leaf or the like falls into a tube, many observers simultaneously perceive [the notions of] whirling, falling, and entering; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of a confusion of universals (*jāti-saṅkara*). However, no such confusion of cognitions is observed in the case of upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the other [motions]. Therefore, the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions regarding upward throwing and so forth are due to a difference in their universals, whereas those regarding exiting and so forth are due to a difference in their effects.
If it is asked: "How can there be a difference in cognitions simultaneously? [the answer follows].

Now, it might be thought that just as there is no confusion of genus (*jāti-saṅkara*), so too there is no simultaneous occurrence of multiple actions; therefore, how can observers simultaneously have the cognitions of whirling, falling, and entering with respect to a single action?

To this we reply: it is not so, because of the difference between the parts and the whole, and because of the distinctions among the conjunctions and disjunctions characterized by the various directions.

For one who perceives the conjunctions and disjunctions of the parts with the spatial directions (dikpradeśa) on the sides in succession, there arises the cognition of "turning. For one who observes the disjunction from the upper part and the conjunction with the lower part of the whole (avayavin), there arises the cognition of "falling. Furthermore, for one who perceives the conjunction within the interior of a tube and the disjunction from the exterior space, there arises the cognition of "entering. Thus, it is established that the difference in cognitions such as "going out" and so forth results from the difference in their effects.

Let it be that there is a distinction in the cognition of upward motion and the rest due to a difference in their genus (*jāti*); however, in the case of exiting and the rest, [the distinction] is due to a difference in their effects (*kārya*).
Is "going-ness" (*gamanatva*) a synonym for "action-ness" (*karmatva*), or is it another general property (*sāmānya*)?
From what does this doubt of yours arise?

Because, just as there is a cognition of "action" with respect to those [motions] such as throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*), there is no distinction in the cognition of "going" with respect to them; therefore, it is understood that it is a synonym for "action-ness."

Since it is designated by a specific name, such as "throwing upwards" (utkṣepaṇa) and so forth, one might think that it must therefore be another general property (sāmānya). This is not so; because it is a synonym for "action-ness" (karmatva).
Just like "selfhood" (ātmatva) and "personhood" (puruṣatva), "going-ness" (gamanatva) is indeed a synonym for action-ness.
Now, for what purpose was the term "going" (gamanam) included under the specific designation? It is not [for the sake of redundancy], because it serves to include whirling and so forth.
The inclusion of "going" was made in order to include whirling, falling, vibrating, and the like, which are not already encompassed by the terms "throwing upward" (utkṣepaṇa) and so on.
Otherwise, it would follow that only those four actions mentioned by their specific designations would be the objects of both the general and specific designations.

Alternatively, let there be another commonality, namely *gamanatva* (the state of being motion). This [commonality] resides only in revolving (*bhramaṇa*) and the like, which are the causes of conjunctions and disjunctions in indefinite directions and locations; and the word "motion" (*gamana*) should be understood as being used figuratively for upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the like, because they share the common property of producing conjunctions and disjunctions in their own substratum.
This is the rule for action as that which is accompanied by the notion of existence (*sat-pratyaya-karma-vidhi*).

How [does this occur]? When one desires to perform sacrifices, study, giving, agriculture, and so forth, and wishes to raise up or lower down the hand, then an effort (*prayatna*) arises in that portion of the self (*ātman*) where the hand is located. From the conjunction of the self and the hand, assisted by gravity (*gurutva*) and disregard (*upekṣā*), motion occurs in the hand. Just as it occurs in the hand, so too does it occur in all the limbs of the body, such as the feet and others, and in the body itself.

How [does it occur] even with respect to those things connected to that? When one grasps a pestle with the hand and forms the desire, "I shall lift up the pestle with my hand," immediately thereafter an effort arises; from the conjunction of the self and the hand depending upon that [effort], at the very same time that the action of lifting arises in the hand, at that same time an action also arises in the pestle from the conjunction of the hand and the pestle depending upon that very same effort.

When the pestle has been raised far from that point, the desire for that purpose ceases, and again the desire to cast it down arises. Immediately following that, an effort [is produced]. Depending upon that effort and the aforementioned conjunction, two simultaneous actions of downward casting occur in the hand and the pestle. Then, by the final action of the pestle, a conjunction called "impact" (abhighāta) is produced between the mortar and the pestle. That conjunction, depending upon the momentum residing in the pestle, produces an upward-throwing action in the pestle which is independent of any other cause.

Depending on that action and the impact, it initiates a *saṃskāra* (elasticity) in the pestle; depending on that, the conjunction of the hand and the pestle produces an upward-moving action even when the [downward] motion has ceased.

Even though the previous *saṃskāra* has perished, nevertheless, the conjunction of the pestle and the mortar is a producer of a potent action because of its specific nature; thus, it becomes capable of assisting in the initiation of that *saṃskāra*. Alternatively, the very same potent *saṃskāra* from before remains undestroyed by the impact and persists.

Therefore, there is no further initiation of a *saṃskāra* in that which already possesses a *saṃskāra*. Consequently, at the very time when the action of upward motion occurs in the pestle due to a blow dependent upon a *saṃskāra*, at that same time, the action of upward motion also occurs in the hand—though it is not caused by an external impulse—due to the contact between the hand and the pestle, depending upon that very same *saṃskāra*.
This is the rule for the movement among those [objects] mentioned in relation to the hand.

How so? When the desire to lift a javelin arises by grasping it with the hand, immediately thereafter an effort [is produced]; depending upon that [effort] and the previously mentioned two types of conjunction, two simultaneous actions of drawing toward oneself occur in the javelin and the hand.

When the hand has been extended, the effort for the purpose of drawing it back ceases. Immediately thereafter, the desire arises, "I shall throw it sideways, upwards, far, or near. Following that, an effort corresponding to that [desire] arises; depending upon that effort, the contact between the hand and the *tomara* (spear), known as *nodana* (impulsion), initiates a momentum (*saṃskāra*) in the *tomara* produced by the action, which depends upon that impulsion. Then, by means of both that momentum and the impulsion, actions continue to occur as long as there is no separation between the hand and the *tomara*. Thereafter, when the impulsion has ceased due to that separation, actions corresponding to the [original] effort—whether sideways, far, or near—occur from the momentum alone until the spear falls.
Similarly, the procedure for movement regarding a mechanical device has been explained.

How so? When a strong man, having practiced his exercises, steadies a bow with his left hand, fits an arrow with his right, and grasps the string along with the arrow in his fist, he forms the desire to draw it, thinking, "I shall draw this strung bow."

Immediately thereafter, when an action of drawing arises in the hand due to the contact between the self and the hand depending upon that effort, at that very same moment, an action arises in the bowstring and the arrow depending upon the contact between the hand, the string, and the arrow depending upon that same effort; and actions arise in the two ends of the bow depending upon the contacts between the string and the ends, which depend upon the contact between the hand, the string, and the arrow characterized by that effort—all of this occurs simultaneously.

Thus, when the bow has been drawn to the ear, there arises the cognition that "it must not be drawn further than this. From that, the effort intended for drawing ceases; subsequently, the desire to release [the arrow] arises. Immediately after that, an effort occurs. Depending upon that effort and the contact between the self and the finger, there is motion in the finger. From that, there is disjunction from the bowstring. From that disjunction, there is the destruction of the contact. When that contact has perished, because of the absence of an obstructing factor, the *sthitisthāpaka* (elasticity) latent in the bow restores the bow—which had become curved—to its original state. At that time, depending upon that very elasticity and the contact between the bow and the string, motion arises in both the string and the arrow. That motion, depending on its own cause, produces an elasticity in the string.

Depending upon that [bow], the conjunction of the arrow and the bowstring is the impulsion (*nodana*). From that, an action (*karman*) arises in the arrow; depending upon that impulsion, it initiates a latent disposition (*saṃskāra*) in the arrow. From that latent disposition, aided by the impulsion, actions continue to occur as long as there is no separation between the arrow and the string. Once the separation occurs and the impulsion has ceased, the subsequent actions arise solely from the latent disposition in the arrow until its fall. Why do many actions occur successively? Because of the multiplicity of conjunctions. However, the latent disposition is single, because there is no cause for dependence on further actions in the interval.
Thus, action has been described as having a real cause or an unreal cause when it is based upon the self.
When it is not so based, in the case of the four external great elements (*mahābhūta*), action occurs without a cause; indeed, motion arises from impulsion (*nodana*) and other such factors.

In that context, impulsion is a particular kind of conjunction which, depending on gravity, fluidity, momentum, and effort—either collectively or individually—is the cause of a single action that serves as the basis for non-disjunction. From that, action occurs in all four great elements.
As in the case of the earth known as "mud.
Impact (*abhighāta*) is that which, depending on momentum, is the cause of a particular conjunction and the cause of a single action that results in disjunction.

Therefore, motion also occurs in the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Just as it occurs when hard objects such as stones are struck, so too it occurs in the earth known as mud when it is pushed or struck by the feet and so forth. That conjunction which depends on either the push or the strike, or on both, is a "conjunction with what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*). From that as well, motion arises in the earth and other elements;
and motion is produced even in those parts that are neither pushed nor struck.
Falling is that downward motion which occurs due to gravity when there is an absence of conjunction, effort, or velocity that counteracts gravity,
as in the case of a pestle, a body, and so forth. Among these, the first [motion] is due to gravity alone, while the second and subsequent ones are due to both gravity and momentum (*saṃskāra*).

The downward flow of water that has become a stream from high ground to low ground occurs because of its fluidity (*dravatva*). How so? Because the fluidity of the whole (*avayavin*) is obstructed by its connection with a surrounding embankment; the fluidity of the parts (*avayava*), which inheres in the same object as that [whole], is likewise obstructed by that very same [embankment]; and the fluidities of the successive parts are obstructed by the conjunctions of those [parts] with one another.

But when a breach of the dam is made by even a small amount [of water], then, because the fluidity of the whole is obstructed on all sides, there is no commencement of the effect; however, for the fluidity of the part situated near the dam, there is the attainment of its function due to the absence of obstruction from the subsequent fluidities of the other parts.

Then, there is the successive movement of those very [atoms] that are conjoined. Thereafter, upon the destruction of the previous substance, a long substance consisting of parts is produced by means of a continuous series. And in that case, fluidity arises through the sequence beginning with the qualities of the causes. Furthermore, when the conjoined causes move in a continuous series, the action that arises in the whole is called "flowing" (*syandana*). Action arising from *saṃskāra* has been explained in the context of arrows and the like.

Likewise, when parts of objects such as wheels produce conjunctions and disjunctions with specific directions and locations on their sides, that action which arises from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the whole (*avayavin*) and causes conjunctions and disjunctions with non-specific directions and locations is called "revolving" (*bhramaṇa*).
Such are the various types of motion.

Regarding the wind called *prāṇa*, its action arises from its conjunction with the bodily wind, depending on an effort preceded by desire and aversion; for in the case of one who is awake, [the movement] is seen to conform to desire, whereas in the case of one who is asleep, it depends on an effort preceded by the mere impulse of life (*jīvana*).

As for ether (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*diś*), and the self (*ātman*), although they possess substantiality (*dravyabhāva*), they are devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*), because, like universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, they are formless (*amūrtatva*).

Form (*mūrti*) is the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading (*asarvagatadravyaparimāṇa*); and action conforms to that [form]. Since that [form] does not exist in ether and the others, there is no connection with action for them.

In the embodied state, for the purpose of connecting the mind with another sense organ, there occurs the action of a waking person due to the conjunction of the self, the mind, and the body, depending on an effort preceded by desire and aversion; this is because we observe the perception of other objects through other sense organs according to one's intention.

At the time of awakening for one who is asleep, it depends on an effort preceded by the life-force (*jīvana*). Furthermore, the actions of exiting (*apasarpaṇa*) and entering (*utsarpaṇa*) [the body] arise from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).

How so? When there is the exhaustion of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the co-factors for life, either through experience or through mutual suppression, then—due to the deficiency of those two co-factors of life and the resulting deficiency of the effort preceded by them—the vital breaths are obstructed. Consequently, by means of the other two [types of] merit and demerit that have attained their functional state, and with the conjunction of the self and the mind as a co-factor, there arises an action of "departure" (*apasarpaṇa-karma*) which causes separation from the dead body.

Then, having departed from that body, it becomes connected with a subtle body (*ativāhika-śarīra*) produced by those very same factors of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). Having transmigrated and reached heaven or hell, it becomes connected with a body corresponding to its latent dispositions (*āśaya*). The movement of karma is for the purpose of that conjunction.
Furthermore, it is the movement of the mind—which has been projected outward by yogis—to a desired location and its return;
likewise, at the time of creation, it is caused by the unseen force of karma (*adṛṣṭa-kārita*) for the purpose of connecting with a newly formed body.

In this same way, whatever else among the great elements has a cause that is not perceived through either direct perception or inference, yet is capable of producing benefit or harm, that too is brought about by the unseen (adṛṣṭa). For example: at the beginning of creation, the motion of atoms; the upward and horizontal movement of fire and wind; the coagulation of the great elements;
and the movement of consecrated gems toward a thief.
And the movement of iron toward a magnet.
Thus concludes the category of action (*karmapadārtha*) in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
Now follows the definition of the category of generality (*sāmānya*).
Generality is of two kinds: the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*).

It pervades its own entire domain, possesses a non-differentiated nature, and subsists in many individuals. It produces a cognition that conforms to its own essential form across one, two, or many [substrata], and by existing continuously in its substrata without distinction from its own form, it is the cause of inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*).

How so? When cognition arises through a continuous series in dependence upon a universal for each individual object, that which persists as a consequence of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the causal conditions of repeated practice and from the reflective observation of the preceding series of cognitions, is the universal.
Among these, the highest universal is existence (*sattā*), which is solely the cause of the notion of inclusion (*anuvṛtti*).

Just as there is a recurrence of the cognition "blue, blue" with respect to mutually distinct things such as skins, clothes, and woolen blankets due to their connection with a single substance that is air (*anila*), so too there is a recurrence of the undifferentiated cognition "existent, existent" with respect to substances, qualities, and actions which are mutually distinct. And since this [cognition] must arise from something other than its objects, that which is the object other [than the individual entities] is established as *sattā* (Being).
Because of the connection with *sattā*, there is the recurrence of the cognition "existent, existent"; therefore, it is indeed a universal (*sāmānya*).

Furthermore, substance-ness (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so forth, are both universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*), because they serve as the causes for both inclusion (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

Among these, substance-ness is a universal because it is the cause of inclusion among earth and the other substances which are mutually distinct, and it is a particular because it is the cause of exclusion from qualities and actions. Likewise, quality-ness is a universal because it is the cause of inclusion among color and the other qualities which are mutually distinct, and it is a particular because it is the cause of exclusion from substances and actions.

Likewise, "action-ness" (*karmatva*) is a generality (*sāmānya*) because it is the cause of a recurring cognition among mutually distinct actions such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), and it is a particular (*viśeṣa*) because it is the cause of differentiation from substances and qualities. In this way, the status of being both a generality and a particular is established for earth-ness, form-ness, upward-throwing-ness, cow-ness, jar-ness, cloth-ness, and so forth, which reside in both living and non-living things, due to their being the causes of recurring and differentiating cognitions. However, these [higher categories] beginning with "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) are primarily generalities because they have a vast range of objects; yet they are called "particulars" figuratively because they differentiate their own substrata.

Due to the difference in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is established that these [universals] are distinct categories (*padārthāntara*) from substance, quality, and action. For this very reason, they are eternal.
Furthermore, they are mutually distinct because of the restriction of their occurrence within substances and so forth, and because of the difference in their cognitions.

Each [universal] is one because there is no distinction in its definition within its own substrata and because it lacks a specific defining characteristic. Although universals have unlimited spatial extent, they nevertheless pervade their entire range of objects due to the restriction of their indicators and the restriction of the causal complex. Furthermore, because the relations of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) do not exist in the intervening space, they cannot be designated [as being there].
Thus ends the category of generality (sāmānya) in the Praśastapādabhāṣya.

Now, the determination of the category of particularity (*viśeṣa*). Those things which exist at the limits [of substance] are "limit-located" (*antya*); they are called "particularities" (*viśeṣa*) because they differentiate their own substrata.

Existing one by one in each eternal substance—which is devoid of destruction or origination, namely atoms, space, time, direction, self, and mind—they are the causes of the cognition of absolute differentiation.

Just as in the case of people like us, a distinction in cognition regarding cows and the like—arising from causes such as common form, quality, action, parts, and conjunction—is observed [when distinguishing them] from horses and the like, as in: "It is a cow," "It is white," "It moves swiftly," "It has a thick hump," and "It has large bells."

Likewise, for yogis superior to us, with respect to eternal atoms—which are identical in form, quality, and activity—and with respect to liberated selves and minds, since no other cause is possible, those causes from which the differentiation of cognitions arises—such that one has the distinct perception "this is distinct" and "that is distinct" with respect to each substrate—and from which recognition arises as "this is that very same atom" despite the remoteness of space and time, are the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*).

Furthermore, if for yogins there were a cessation of [erroneous] cognition and recognition arising from the dharma produced by yoga (*yogaja-dharma*) even without the ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*), what would follow? It is not the case that such occurs.
Just as from the dharma produced by yoga, a cognition of white does not arise regarding what is not white, nor does recognition occur regarding that which has never been seen before;
if it were to occur, it would be false—so too here, for yogins, a cessation of cognition or recognition cannot possibly occur from the dharma produced by yoga without the ultimate particularity.

If it is asked: "Why is the exclusion of cognition not postulated as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*) in the case of atoms, just as it is in the case of ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*)?"—the answer is: no, because of identity (*tādātmya*).

In this world, with respect to things that do not possess that nature [of being a particular], a cognition arises due to another cause, such as [the cognition of] jars and the like arising from a lamp; but in the case of a lamp, it does not arise from another lamp.

Just as the impurity of beef, horse-flesh, and so forth is intrinsic, while for others it is due to contact with them, so too here, because of identity, the exclusion of cognition is intrinsic to ultimate particulars, while for atoms and the like it is due to contact with them.
Thus ends the category of particularity (*viśeṣa*) in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
Now follows the definition of the category of inherence (*samavāya*).

Inherence is that relation between things that are inseparably connected (*ayutasiddha*) and exist in the relationship of the supported and the support (*ādhāryādhārabhūta*), which is the cause of the cognition "it is here. It is that relation—called inherence—from which there arises the notion "this is in that" regarding substances, qualities, motions, universals, and particulars, whether they stand in a causal relationship or not, provided they are inseparably connected and exist as the supported and the support; and it is that from which there occurs the non-separation (*aviṣvagbhāva*) of non-pervasive entities whose distinctness has been apprehended.

How so? Just as the cognition "curd is in this bowl" is observed when a relation exists, so too, because we observe such cognitions as "the cloth is in these threads," "the mat is in these vīraṇa-grasses," "quality and action are in this substance," "existence is in substances, qualities, and actions," "substantiality is in this substance," "quality-ness is in this quality," "action-ness is in this action," and "ultimate particularities are in this eternal substance," it is known that a relation between these [categories] exists.

Furthermore, this conjunction does not exist because the related entities are inseparable (ayutasiddha), because the causes such as the action of one of the two are impossible, because no end in disjunction is observed, and because there exists only the relationship between the locus and that which is to be located.

And this [inherence] is a distinct category from substance and the others, because its definition differs, just like existence (*bhāva*). Just as existence, substanceness (*dravyatva*), and so forth, are distinct entities from their own substrates and from one another—because they produce cognitions corresponding to their own natures in their respective loci—so too inherence is a distinct category from those [other] five categories, because the cognition "it is here" is observed in respect to them. Furthermore, it does not possess plurality like conjunction, because its indicative mark is non-different from that of existence and because there is no specific indicative mark [for plurality]. Therefore, like existence, inherence is one and the same everywhere.

Now, if inherence (*samavāya*) is one, then because it is a single relation with the qualifiers such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*) in relation to substances, qualities, and actions, does it not follow that there would be a confusion of categories (*padārthasaṅkara*)? No, because of the restriction between the locus and the located (*ādhārādheyaniyama*).
Although inherence is one and independent in all cases, there is nevertheless a restriction between the locus and the located.
How so? Substantiality exists only in substances; quality-ness exists only in qualities; and action-ness exists only in actions.
Why is it so? Because of the observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Here, because the positive concomitance of the cognition whose cause is inherence (*samavāya*) is observed, it is understood that inherence is one and the same everywhere.
Because the negative concomitance of the causes such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth is observed, their specific restriction is known.
Just as there is a restriction regarding the relationship between locus and located (āśrayāśrayibhāva) despite the oneness of the conjunction between a bowl and its curd,

so too, even though inherence (samavāya) is one, there is a restriction regarding the container and the contained among categories such as substantiality (dravyatva) and the like, due to the distinction between their capacities as the manifestor (vyañjaka) and the manifested (vyaṅgya).
Even though the relation is eternal, it does not possess impermanence like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because, like existence (*bhāva*), it is without cause.
Just as it has been stated that existence is eternal because no cause for it is perceived through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too is inherence (*samavāya*).
For no cause whatsoever for this [inherence] is perceived through valid cognition.
By what kind of occurrence (*vṛtti*), moreover, does inherence (*samavāya*) subsist in substances and so forth?

It cannot be conjunction (*samyoga*), because that, being a quality (*guṇa*), is dependent upon a substance. Nor can it be inherence itself, because inherence is unitary (*ekatva*). And there is no other mode of occurrence. [To this we reply: No.

Because of identity (*tādātmya*). Just as for substances, qualities, and actions—which are of the nature of the existent (*sat*)—there is no other connection with existence (*sattā*), so too for inherence (*samavāya*), which is indivisible and consists of the mode of subsistence (*vṛttyātmaka*), there is no other mode of subsistence; therefore, its subsistence is within its own self.

Therefore, inherence is beyond the senses, because it does not function in perceptible objects—just as existence (*sattā*) and other such categories do not—and because there is no self-cognition (*svātmagatasaṃvedana*) of it.
Consequently, inherence is to be inferred through the cognition of "here" (*ihabuddhi*).
Thus ends the category of inherence (*samavāya*) in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
Homage to that Kaṇabhuj, who, having satisfied Maheśvara by means of the power of his yoga practice, composed the Vaiśeṣika treatise.
Thus ends the *Bhāṣya* on the six categories, beginning with substance, composed by Praśastapāda.
